madam president, i shall refer to the breyer report. i have to say that european farmers are fully aware that when using plant protection products particular attention must be paid to human health and also to the protection of the environment. however, the sector is deeply concerned that the european parliament does not understand the impact this regulation may have in the future. the fact is that there are assessments of its potential impact which indicate that, due to the future scarcity of plant protection products, it will be very difficult to control pests and diseases affecting the cultivation of a large number of foodstuffs, in particular all mediterranean products, and also the cultivation of ornamental plants and cut flowers. i am fully aware that the agreement reached in the tripartite dialogue was the result of arduous negotiation and i can therefore only acknowledge the work done by the rapporteurs. but it must be borne in mind that the temporary definition of endocrine disruptors will lead to the disappearance of a large number of active substances, especially insecticides, of key importance for agriculture. producers need to have at their disposal a sufficient quantity of active substances to effectively and safely combat any plant disease or pest, bearing in mind that often the danger is not in the product itself but in the misuse of the product. the spanish delegation of the epp-ed group therefore supports the proposals calling for an impact assessment and will vote in favour of mr sturdy's amendments, which i myself have signed, on endocrine disruptors and those favouring the availability of plant protection products in case of emergency. moreover, if this regulation is adopted under the terms of the agreement reached, the effects will be a reduction in food production and a rise in prices which will lead us to import the same foodstuffs which we do not produce but which are treated with the products we are banning.

the rapporteur, mr president, the directive to which the report refers is an amendment to a 1978 directive on the same subject, drawn up in the light of the treaty of amsterdam, the case law developed by the court of justice of the european communities and new social realities; an amendment incorporating key elements in the advancement of women's rights, which are the ones assessed in this report. the legal text introduces the definition of direct and indirect discrimination, harassment and sexual harassment, requires member states to encourage employers to take measures to prevent all forms of discrimination on grounds of sex and safeguards employment rights after maternity or paternity leave. in implementing this directive, member states, in addition to committing themselves to the creation of equality bodies with functions of promotion, analysis, implementation and support of equal treatment, undertake to implement social dialogue, with the aim of promoting equal treatment in the world of work through collective agreements and in a planned manner. they also undertake to strengthen the role of ngos in promoting equality, to establish effective sanctioning measures for those who do not comply with the provisions of the directive and to implement protection measures for those who provide support to victims. if the commission had been able to draw up the report which, according to the directive itself, is required every four years, our evaluation work would have been relatively simple. to do so, all member states would have to have transposed the directive within the deadline, done so correctly and sent all the information to the commission. but this was not the situation we started from. at the end of the transposition period, nine member states had not notified the measures taken to transpose the directive; the commission had opened infringement proceedings against them and, as of may last year, proceedings were still open against two member states. in addition, due to the complexity and novel aspects of the directive, the commission had identified transposition problems in 22 member states, although it hoped to resolve many of them through dialogue. in order to produce a report that was as rigorous, useful and as complete as possible, we needed more data, so we decided to ask the member states for information as well. with the information provided by the commission, the information received from the member states - through the equality bodies and the national parliaments - and with the input of my colleagues from the various groups, we have been able to draw up this report, which already gives a clear picture of how the transposition process is developing in each of the member states. i would like to point out that, in the light of experience, cooperation between the national parliaments and the european parliament has been essential to our success. without the information provided by the parliaments and equality bodies we would not have been able to produce this report, at least not with the depth with which we have done so; nor would it have been possible without the fluid collaboration we have been able to establish with the commission and the invaluable help of the services of the committee on women's rights and gender equality, my office and the services of my parliamentary group. to all of them - because they are women - i want to thank you. i would also like to thank the speakers for their contributions and their willingness to do so. our aim from the outset was to ensure that our work was not only rigorous and useful but also the result of maximum consensus, since it was a question of getting a good picture of the situation regarding the transposition of a very important directive, which provides the european union with very effective tools for the member states to strengthen their legislation on equal treatment in the field of employment, something which is fundamental to achieving the objectives we have set ourselves as europeans. let us not forget that there is still a 28.4 percentage point difference between the employment rate of men and women in the european union today, that we are still far from the lisbon target of 60% female employment by 2010 and that women are paid on average 15% less than men. if this report also serves to raise awareness in the member states on this matter, we can be doubly pleased.

the next item is the report by marco cappato, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on public access to european parliament, council and commission documents (application of regulation (ec) no 1049/2001) (a6-0459/2008).
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, i wish to begin by thanking you for a very well-written and interesting report, and i congratulate the rapporteur. this is an important and cherished subject, particularly in times of the revision of regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 and also bearing in mind the changes that the treaty of lisbon – if it enters into force – will bring about on these important issues. this report is in principle about the implementation of regulation 1049/2001 and, therefore, let me start by recalling one of the positive elements in the implementation of the regulation because, as the quantitative data show and as the parliament report acknowledges, the eu institutions have granted access to a higher number of documents while registering a decrease in the number and rate of refusals. we are committed to continuing to enhance transparency and openness. quite naturally, some of the recommendations made in the report go well beyond the application of regulation 1049/2001 in 2006 and some are not directly related to the activities of the commission, as we have just heard. the report addresses a number of issues concerning openness and communication with citizens, and i particularly welcome that as a valuable input for a general reflection on transparency, communication and outreach. let me just briefly go through some of the recommendations and the principles underpinning them, because they deserve due consideration. on the turco case, i can assure you that the commission takes this judgment fully into account. as has been said, it mainly concerns the need for increased openness where the council acts in its legislative capacity, but it is also applicable to the commission and all the institutions, and the commission makes sure that each request for access is carefully assessed on a case-by-case basis against the parameters set by the court of justice. secondly, the proposal to lay down common rules on administrative procedures requires more reflection because many of these procedures are very specific in nature and unique, in some cases, for every institution. this means that we will need some more time to see how that could be done. the recommendation to merge regulation 1049/2001 and regulation (eec, euratom) no 354/83 on the opening of the historical archives is quite complex for a particular reason, because article 255 of the ec treaty and regulation 1049/2001 do not apply to all institutions and bodies. this might also change if and when the lisbon treaty enters into force, because it will then extend the right of access to documents to all institutions and bodies. this is why it is not so easy to simply merge the two, because the coverage is different. on the ombudsman’s critical remark regarding the commission’s public registers, i would like to assure you that we take this remark very seriously. as you know, we have a public register of documents that has been up and running since june 2002 and since then the commission has also put in place a dedicated register for comitology procedures and a register on expert groups. we are always doing our utmost to modernise our internal it systems. this, unfortunately, will not happen overnight, but has to be worked on. we always take into account the need to increase the coverage of the public register, and i hope you also know my personal commitment to this. we acknowledge that we still have to increase the coverage of our public registers and we confirm our commitment to develop the public registers in the interests of enhanced transparency. in the resolution you target the questions of document management and a common portal and the trans-jai project. the commission supports the idea of setting up a common portal in order to facilitate access for citizens to legislative documents. i think this would entail a common methodology, and we have to look at all the practical consequences of that on document identification and references. we would like to see a portal that could entail the full availability of public documents for each institution, so we are willing to work together with you on that. on the trans-jai project, i come back to what i said in a reply in october, that this is expected to be open to the general public by 2010. let me also comment on the issue of exchange of information between the institutions. i understand what is meant there and what you are after, but i wish to remind you that between our institutions we already have an established working method with the exchange of confidential information held by the commission and this is regulated in an annex to the framework agreement. we should also keep in mind that the question of sharing information between institutions is not related to public access and we think that this should be handled separately, as it is currently. this report and the debate is also a valuable and appreciated input for another time when we can discuss it on a broader scale. i am grateful for parliament’s efforts to keep the issue of transparency and openness high on the eu agenda. we will come back to many of these questions in the very near future, for instance during the joint meeting of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs with the czech parliament next week which i shall have the pleasure to attend, and then in just a couple of weeks we will be dealing with the important issue of revising regulation 1049/2001. i think the discussions should not end there. we need to be open about transparency and think also what we can do proactively outside the formal legislation, such as on improved registers, on greater user-friendliness and accessibility, active dissemination and quicker publication of documents. something that i myself did last year was to make the register of my own correspondence directly accessible on the web. i am sure that you all have similar ideas and examples of what can be done if we just put our minds to it. so let us do that.

president-in-office of the council. − mr president, thank you very much for giving me the floor in this timely debate on the dramatic situation in the middle east. since the start of israel’s military campaign in the gaza strip on 27 december, we have witnessed a steep deterioration of the situation on all levels. the humanitarian consequences of this operation are dramatic for the population in gaza. since the start of the operation, over 900 palestinians have died, of whom roughly 30% were women and children. we are profoundly disturbed by the loss of civilian life, and the matter has been repeatedly declared in our presidential statements. the european union deplores the ongoing hostilities which have led to such high numbers of civilian casualties, and we want to express our sincere condolences to the families of the victims. we are particularly concerned by such incidents as the attack on the united nations school in jebaliya and the firing on humanitarian convoys leading to the death of humanitarian staff. over 4 200 palestinians have been injured, according to the office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs. according to the united nations agency, an estimated 28 000 people have been displaced since the beginning of the hostilities. a large number of them are seeking refuge in the shelters; the rest of the internally displaced people are staying with relatives. the greatest humanitarian needs are related to the large number of wounded and the overwhelmed health services, whereas displaced people and host families need specific assistance such as food, shelter, water and non-food items. since the water system was badly damaged and needs urgent repair, the gaza population has hardly any access to safe water. therefore, providing drinking water is of the utmost necessity. there are also extensive food shortages at all levels of the population. since 4 november last year, foreign ngos’ personnel have not been allowed access to gaza to deliver and monitor humanitarian aid properly. also, the number of trucks entering gaza has increased since military operations started. the current daily average of 55 trucks remains pitifully insufficient compared to a need for at least 300 trucks daily to cover the needs of the 80% of the population which has become aid-dependent. the european union has been closely following the tragic events from the outset. three days after the operation started, foreign ministers met in an extraordinary session in paris to discuss the situation. they agreed on the need for an immediate and permanent ceasefire and immediate humanitarian action in stepping up the peace process. the summit aimed mainly to assist in ending violence and alleviating the humanitarian crisis. the presidency led a diplomatic mission in the middle east. the eu ministerial troika visited the region on 4-6 january for meetings in egypt, in israel, with the palestinian authority, and in jordan. the high representative also visited syria, lebanon and turkey. the outlines of a solution to the crisis have started to emerge. first and foremost, there must be an unconditional halt to rocket attacks by hamas on israel and an end to israeli military action, to enable the sustained delivery of humanitarian aid and the restoration of public services and badly-needed medical treatment. the six-month ceasefire, which expired on 19 december, was far from perfect. israel suffered through periodic rocket fire and the knowledge that its foe was amassing greater firepower. gaza endured a really punishing economic blockade, totally undermining its economic development.in order to achieve a sustainable ceasefire, we have to look for a sensible compromise entailing an end to rocket launches and reopening of the crossings. a viable solution must address the tunnels across the borders, especially along the philadelphia route, to prevent the smuggling of weapons. it must also lead to the systematic and controlled opening of all border crossings to enable the gaza economy to develop. we believe that the deployment of international missions to monitor implementation of the ceasefire and to act as a liaison between the two sides could be helpful. in this regard, the european union is ready to return its observers to the rafah crossing and to extend the mandate of the european border mission in scope and content. we acknowledge that israel has agreed to a daily lull to allow desperately-needed food, fuel and medicine into gaza. however, only a full and immediate ceasefire would allow the delivery and distribution of the large quantities of humanitarian aid that gaza so desperately needs and for the resumption of basic services. israel must ensure the unhindered and safe access for humanitarian aid and other essential supplies, including food, medicines and fuel, to the palestinian civilian population of the gaza strip, as well as the safe passage of civilian persons and humanitarian personnel into and from the gaza strip. but even a durable and comprehensive solution in gaza will not be sufficient to install peace in the region. we need to address broader and more complicated challenges. we need a new and inclusive strategy that addresses the internal palestinian political situation, as well as a resumption of the peace talks which have been suspended due to the gaza crisis. palestinian reconciliation, and a government representative of the aspirations of the palestinian people, is more necessary than ever. we therefore support the mediation effort undertaken by egypt in accordance with the arab league’s resolutions of 26 november 2008. as pointed out in the conclusions of the gaerc in december 2008, the european union is prepared to support any stable palestinian government that pursues policies and measures reflecting the quartet’s principles. the european union stresses the need to achieve a just, lasting and comprehensive peace in the middle east and calls for the resumption of palestinian-israeli negotiations and the resolving of all outstanding issues in the israeli-palestinian conflict, including all core issues. a durable and comprehensive solution will ultimately depend on real progress in the middle east peace process. urgent and great efforts by the parties will be needed to achieve a comprehensive peace, based on the vision of a region where two democratic states, israel and palestine, live side by side in peace, in secure and recognised borders. the latest outbreak of violence in the middle east might not only set back prospects of a peaceful settlement in the conflict between israel and palestine. the political damage the fighting is causing, both in terms of regional polarisation and radicalisation, and in the further discrediting of moderate forces, must not be neglected either. only a viable palestinian state will bring security to a region that has suffered for too long. this is especially in the interests of israel and its neighbours. therefore, urgent measures must immediately be taken to reverse the damage done by the military action in order to restore the possibility of an equitable negotiated outcome. (applause)
member of the commission. − mr president, i think we all would have hoped for a better start to 2009. unfortunately, we face a terrible and appalling conflict in gaza, which is now in its third week. it gives cause for immense concern. we discussed it yesterday at a meeting with the committee on foreign affairs, the committee on development and those members of the european parliament who had been in gaza at the weekend. the president-in-office of the council has already mentioned the terrible statistics of the dead and injured, which get worse every day. there is increasing evidence of victims suffering from extreme burns, and aid agencies report that the population is suffering from acute shortages of food, fuel and medicine, not to mention the destruction of houses and infrastructure. suffering, and this war is no exception. therefore, beyond its immediate devastating impact, it pushes the prospect of peace much further away, undermines the arab peace initiative and could potentially have a very negative impact on the stability of the whole region. i should like to outline quickly the diplomatic activity that we have taken together to bring this conflict to an end, and then to look at the mid- and long-term challenges. we have been active from day one, which i think was important. we know that we are not the main player in the middle east, but we were, and are, an member of the commission. - mr president, mr mep, ladies and gentlemen, i fully agree with the honourable member that the way we treat animals, including farm animals, is both an ethical issue and undoubtedly a question of civilization. the commission is aware that the transport of animals for commercial purposes can cause serious suffering to animals. such suffering is particularly pronounced in the case of so-called low-value animals such as slaughter animals. the enforcement of long-distance transport legislation is not satisfactory. in recent months, the commission has received reports of cases of animal cruelty. the commission continues to support the best available options to improve the situation. the ultimate objective is to improve the enforcement of european union legislation and thus to improve animal health and welfare of the animals concerned. a study carried out by the joint research centre concluded that new and more efficient control systems, such as the tracking of transport by satellite positioning systems, could contribute to improving the situation and allow for more transparent implementation of the rules. the use of these new technologies would also contribute to reducing the administrative burden on national authorities and bodies. the commission is also considering the possibility of proposing, before the end of this mandate, new standards based on the results of scientific research on transport duration, the number of animals loaded and the number of animals loaded in vehicles. the commission assesses the implementation of european union legislation on the basis of reports provided by member states in accordance with the existing eu regulation. the information contained in those reports shall be combined with the results of on-the-spot checks carried out in the member states by veterinary experts. the results of these checks carried out by the commission experts are published on the commission's website. data are also considered in the context of reports issued by international non-governmental organisations active in this field. the vast majority of member states have already submitted to the commission their animal transport reports for 2007. by the end of 2008, cyprus, lithuania, malta, bulgaria and luxembourg had not yet submitted their reports. the commission has drawn their attention to this obligation and will continue to monitor the situation closely. however, regulation (ec) no 1/2005 does not require the commission to draw up a report on the enforcement of the regulation in the member states. the commission agrees that enforceability is a key aspect of any proposed legislation. consequently, the commission would take account of the analysis of member states' reports for possible future revisions of community legislation in this area.

member of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to begin by stressing the importance of a healthy diet for preventing disease. as members of the european parliament you are aware that the white paper 'a strategy for europe on nutrition, overweight and obesity-related health problems', adopted by the european commission on 30 may 2007, brings together all the community policies that can contribute to improving eating habits and preventing obesity. these are in particular measures in the fields of public health, nutrition, transport, regional policy, sport, education, statistics and agricultural policy. one of the best examples is the commission's initiative of a pan-european school fruit and vegetable scheme. the goal of this program is to help us facilitate a healthier start to life for our children. it will start at the beginning of the 2009/2010 school year with an annual budget of eur 90 million for the purchase and supply of fresh fruit and vegetables to schools. as regards the specific question raised by one of the members of parliament, namely the request to include the mediterranean diet in the unesco world heritage list, commissioner kyprianou's predecessor, mr markos kyprianou, raised this issue at the agriculture council in july 2007. the commission welcomes this initiative as it can contribute to promoting healthy eating habits throughout the european union. however, the european commission does not have formal authority to support such a request within unesco, as it is not a member of unesco and therefore cannot participate in the decision-making process. i hope, however, that the participating states will succeed in their application to unesco and that they will receive the appropriate support from the other member states of the european union.

we now come to the point of incidental requests for the president to speak, and we have a problem, because many members have asked to speak. i shall therefore apply absolutely rigorously the decision of the bureau that five members shall be allowed to speak and that the floor shall be automatically cut off when the minutes allocated to each of them have expired.
i would like to take 30 seconds to explain to the honourable members what the rule has been set by the bureau of the house, because i understand that it is very unpleasant for those who ask to speak not to have the floor. what the bureau decided was that the fundamental debate time is the time allotted to those members who speak using the time allocated between the various parliamentary groups and then, on this 'incidental request for intervention' part-session, five members are given the floor, at the rate of one minute each, in order from largest to smallest per group, so that if six ask for it, if there are six minutes, it can be done. and it can be extended to six minutes, maybe seven. but in this case there were 12 members who had asked to speak and therefore only five have been allowed to speak, which is what the bureau has established for this point of the debate. i say this so that you may also take it into consideration at a later time. i now call on mr wondra to respond to the various interventions on behalf of the council. mr. minister, you have the floor.
yes, mr konrad, of course you have every right to protest and we have noted your protest. but you, who belong to a very responsible group in this house, will understand that it cannot be that individual members have more time than the groups, which are the ones who have the statutory responsibility to take part in the debates. the bureau took this decision unanimously. it is a decision which i consider to be common sense, in order to prevent people who do not sign up for the group, because their group does not give them the floor at that moment, from intervening later, so that the time was cut down: five minutes for five speeches, by order of the group, from the largest to the smallest, also making sure that they are not all of the same nationality. that's what was decided. of course, that rule can be changed. if the conference of presidents suggests to the bureau a change in procedure, the bureau will consider it with great interest. thank you very much, mr konrad, for your speech, which we take note of. the debate is closed. written declarations (article 142 of the regulation)

on behalf of the alde group. mr president, today in europe citizens travel without borders, can vote in a state other than their own, can collect their pension, have social security in any state in which they decide to reside - not only that: the police cooperate with each other or a prosecutor in stockholm can arrest, thanks to the euroorder, a person living in seville without any need to process anything directly. when it comes to repressing the behaviour of citizens, states have been wise to let their sovereignty slip. but when it comes to leaving the european union and protecting citizens, those same european citizens, as if using a time machine, see that time stops as soon as they leave the union. and outside the union we have 27 states, 27 administrations, 27 flags, 27 consular systems or, in some cases, not even that. and when there is a crisis, the european citizen ceases to be a european citizen. there is no such thing as european citizenship. and those 180 million europeans who travel the world realize that they can only be protected if they become germans, spaniards, poles or italians again. because as europeans we do not exist outside the european union. and that is a serious breach of the treaty and makes science fiction - i say this with all due respect - of the council statement just made. everything the council has told us about the alleged implementation of article 20 of the treaty, 'lead state', videoconferences, joint centres, is pure science fiction when one is in an emergency situation and 'as the commissioner has said' some of us have had the opportunity to experience that in practice. article 20 of the treaty is a blank piece of paper: there are no protocols of action; there are no legal rules; there is no information for the citizen; there is no responsibility for those who decide not to comply with it. at best, there is charity among the consuls. there is goodwill, as there could have been in the 19th century, as there could have been in beijing in 1800. that is the situation: complicity between consuls who eat and dine together and not the obligation to serve citizens together under a provision of european law. and so the european commission has an obligation, even before the lisbon treaty comes into force and, of course, after article 20 is implemented, to make european citizens feel proud of their passport and to make some officials feel that the 19th century is over and that europe also exists as such, in new delhi, in beirut and wherever it is needed, and wherever there is a european citizen in trouble.

the next item is the report by mr friedrich-wilhelm graefe zu baringdorf, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the marketing and use of feedingstuffs (com (2008) 0124 - c6-0128/2008 - 2008/0050 (cod)) (a6-0407/2008).
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner, as i did at the meeting of the committee on agriculture, i would first of all like to congratulate the rapporteur, the other group alternate rapporteurs and the council on the work they have done. the work that has enabled us to reach agreement at first reading has also been an excellent exercise in the codecision procedure, which will be the usual procedure in our committee in the near future. at present, ladies and gentlemen, the legislation on the movement of feed materials and compound feed for animals, including pet animals, - a sector which represents a turnover of some eur 50 billion at community level - is regulated by many directives and some 50 amending or implementing acts. simplification of the rules and harmonized application of the rules are the main objectives, which this regulation will undoubtedly achieve. in 2006, the committee on agriculture of this parliament had already discussed the marketing of feed. at that time, as everyone will remember, we unanimously asked the european commission to find the right balance in the future review between the interest of farmers in having detailed information on ingredients and the interest of industry in having sufficient protection for their know-how. the compromise reached on the main sensitive points of the commission proposal, the open declaration of raw materials and the creation of the community catalogue of raw materials reflect well, in my view, this balance. the positive response to the commitment by all parties involved is proof of this. the undertaking does indeed allow, in the open declaration, to preserve the right of buyers to be informed and that of manufacturers to ownership of their know-how, by stating that the information must be provided without prejudice to the 2004 directive on intellectual property rights. there is no doubt, ladies and gentlemen, that in a relationship of trust between supplier and user the formulas are known, but it would be illogical to be obliged to give the recipe to the first customer who appears at the door. many of us have been drinking coca-cola for years, we do not know the recipe and yet we have no doubt that the characteristics and the health standards are respected. the court of justice's judgment cited above states, in the negative, that the obligation to inform customers who so request of the exact composition of their feedingstuffs is not justified by the objective of protecting health which it pursues. that said, i would like to remind you that the competent authority will be able to have access at any time to the exact composition and that, as stated in the undertaking reached, any urgency relating to human or animal health or the environment will allow the buyer to be provided with accurate information on the composition of the food concerned, after weighing the legitimate interests of both manufacturers and buyers. as regards the catalogue of good labelling practices, the voluntary nature of this instrument at the service of the professionals in the sector is maintained without at any time becoming a positive list of raw materials for the manufacture of compound feedingstuffs, because this is something that we had not been asked to do. the rules will, however, include, at the request of the european parliament, a new annex containing a list of raw materials whose placing on the market or use for animal feed is prohibited or restricted, a catalogue or annex or a list which the commission may keep up to date. the group of the european socialists, my group, which i represent, ladies and gentlemen, supports the compromise reached and has not tabled any amendments to the report. we are in full agreement with the position as it is presented here today in this house and we shall therefore vote in favour of it.
member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank everyone for their remarks, and shall now reply to some of those remarks. first of all, on the question of safety, safety of feed is guaranteed by the negative list of feed materials which cannot be used in feeds. the proposal contains the list of feed materials which are forbidden. the commission will extend that list every time it is convinced that it is necessary to add to that negative list. on the other hand, i wish to remind you that there is a large list of maximum levels of contaminants, such as dangerous micro-toxins, heavy metals and dioxins, which has been in force, under the directive on undesirable substances, since 2002. i would agree with all those who said, as i confirmed, that european food is safe. however, as i also indicated last night during our discussions, laws and regulations are as good as we make them, and we therefore have to remain vigilant and see to it that member states, feed dealers and, indeed, the commission ensure that everybody sticks to their obligations in ensuring that laws really are enforced and that they are good laws. the recent irish meat incident highlights the need for stringent enforcement and controls on legal requirements, and my services will continue to examine how that can be improved. i am confident that, once the new rules come into force, regulation of the feed market will be significantly improved, in the interests of both feed manufacturers and users. last but not least, i would like to thank the rapporteur once again for his excellent contribution, and all members for their constructive and positive role in reaching an agreement on this important initiative.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place at 12 noon today.

the rapporteur. - mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, mr president, reconciling the proper maintenance of ecosystems with the sustainable exploitation of marine resources, preventing and problem') is a good description of the situation, i will not be the one to say that research in the fisheries sector is over-funded, but that we have a double problem. on the one hand, commissioner, when submitting projects to the seventh framework programme: problems which are partly attributable to the different approach required, on the one hand, by aquaculture, which is essentially industrial in nature, and, on the other, by research in fisheries and marine sciences, which is multidisciplinary in nature and which is more long-term. until the seventh framework programme, these two fields were covered by the same funds and were under the responsibility of dg fisheries, allowing for their complementarity. the current dg research is in charge and the result is that it is proving difficult for the scientific community to convey the concerns and needs of the sector to the officials who draw up the call guidelines. on the other hand, there is a certain perception in the scientific community that this directorate-general seems to have chosen to prioritise basic research without giving room to research focused on public policy. i will give you an example: to enrich the community's maritime strategy from a scientific point of view or to investigate the relationship between fishing and climate change. in summary, the european union's maritime policy objective of achieving productive fisheries in a clean marine environment requires access for scientists working in this field to horizontal funding mechanisms in the seventh framework programme. i would like to conclude by referring to the second problem: the worrying shortage of young scientists in fisheries research, which seems to be the result of careers that are not very attractive compared with other basic sciences. it seems indispensable to establish interesting and rewarding university courses that offer good career opportunities. it also seems necessary to harmonise the different applied research models in force in the various member states, in order to be able to compare results better and to facilitate the aggregation of data, and to intensify cooperation between national research institutes. and i certainly think it is essential to integrate fishermen's experience and expertise more closely into the process of drawing up scientific opinions on which to base policy decisions under the cfp.

mr president, i think that the debate we are having tonight serves to clarify a few things: firstly, the fact that the debate on european private enterprise is being held simultaneously with the debate on the european small enterprise does not mean that the european private enterprise is necessarily a european small enterprise. as mrs van den burg has said and i think mr wurtz has also stressed in his criticism of the proposal, the statute of the european private company, as conceived in the commission's proposal and as approved by the committee on legal affairs, is an instrument for the establishment of companies which can be large and which have certain characteristics, such as the limitation of the liability of the partners and the impossibility of their being traded on public markets. but both the european and the national private company statute can be used for small and large companies. as mrs van den burg has said, it is precisely this flexibility or plasticity of european private society that requires us to be extremely careful. and that has been the work of the committee on legal affairs. the amendments adopted by the committee on legal affairs, which are quite numerous, are aimed precisely at preventing the emergence, as mrs van den burg said, of a european delaware on the basis of the formula of the european private company, especially in one of the areas which concerned mr wurtz, that is, the participation of workers in the company. i think that the formulas adopted by the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights clearly indicate these limitations. it is not a question, as mr wurtz said, of applying the country of origin rule, but that, in accordance with the rules we have adopted in the committee on legal affairs - i would recommend mr wurtz to read the amendments we have adopted - there are a number of limitations which prevent the country of origin rules from being applied to those companies in which there is a higher than normal level of worker participation. they are perfectly included in the amendments which we have adopted and i think that with these amendments it would be perfectly permissible to adopt the text, even from mr wurtz's point of view. in other words, it is a form of european company which exists in all our countries and which must be harmonised within the framework of the european union, but in so doing these companies cannot become ethereal entities, but must adhere to national realities and respect national legislation, especially in the very delicate field of worker co-management. i think that the committee on legal affairs has made some fundamental contributions to the text it has adopted and it would certainly be wrong for the commission to ignore these amendments. i believe that the amendments tabled by the committee on legal affairs are aimed precisely at limiting the shortcomings of the commission's text and i believe that parliament could adopt it in good conscience, not only because of the progress it represents in the field of small enterprises but also in terms of the management of such companies which exist in law and which would be subject to strict control by the workers in a system of co-management.

the rapporteur. - madam president, at this late hour on monday the commission will probably have other things to worry about than this report. in short, we are merely responding to a report from the commission, a report on the application of council regulation (ec) no 1206/2001 of 28 may 2001 on cooperation between the courts of the member states in the taking of evidence in civil or commercial matters. we are in a field which is really not community, it is an intergovernmental field, in which the council - through the regulation - has tried to stimulate cooperation between these courts. but in doing so, i think there is a certain lack of rigour on the part of the european union. i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this, but i am saying that it should be involved in the work of the european parliament. i do not know what the commission has achieved or intends to achieve, but i think it is rather difficult to achieve because of the enormous difficulty of this form of intergovernmental cooperation. i mean, we're asking the judicial authorities to collaborate with each other, we're talking about 27 countries, judicial authorities that handle 22 different languages, with very different legal systems from each other, and we're trying to get results. the commission has noted that the results are not good, that there is a huge backlog in these cooperation mechanisms and, of course, that we do not have the means to do so. ideally, we should have material means. for example, what could the commission do to equip the courts, especially lower level courts, with technological elements such as a videoconferencing system? now. parliament, council and commission are much more open now than ever before. you could say that the change of rules led to a change of practice and to a change of minds and attitudes. at the same time, parliament, council and commission also agree that legitimate interests have received adequate protection. we should not forget that the eu institutions have granted access to a higher number of documents, while a decrease in the number and rate of refusals has been registered. so i hope you agree that regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 has proven its value. for this reason a complete overhaul is not necessary. having said this, even a good tool can always be improved. the legal base we have as our starting point is article 255 of the treaty, as has already been mentioned by the rapporteur. following that, the regulation shall define principles and the limits governing the citizen’s right of access to documents. as regards the report at hand, i note that some amendments go beyond the scope of article 255 of the treaty and therefore these amendments cannot be accepted. but – and this is an important ‘but’ – they point to important issues that may well be addressed in another context. the commission will certainly look at that with a constructive, pragmatic and open mind. it is good practice to assess from time to time whether legislation works well and achieves its objectives, and it is in this spirit that the commission drafted its proposal for a recast of the regulation. the use of the recast technique meets the objective of better lawmaking. since this regulation touches upon a fundamental right of citizens, it is of the utmost importance to adopt a single, clear and readable legal text. the recast technique does not tie the hands of the legislator more than the traditional way of amending legislation. irrespective of the choice of legislative technique, the community legislator may not go beyond the aim of the proposal. we are committed to continuing to enhance transparency and openness, and i firmly believe that this is a good way to do it. in this context, however, i have to mention that a number of the amendments concern provisions of regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 which the commission did not propose to amend. we are not in a position to accept them because they go beyond the scope of the commission’s proposal. having said this, the commission is, of course, willing to take on board good ideas, although we are at the moment still in the early stages of the procedure. i would like to confirm that the commission is willing to have discussions with the two co-legislators and that we want to try to find common ground in order to reach a balanced and workable compromise text. however, the commission prefers to come forward with an amended proposal when the two co-legislators have stated their position. we cannot and will not prejudge or anticipate discussions or negotiations. we should also bear in mind the changes that the lisbon treaty – if and when it enters into force – will bring about on this important issue. regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 will then apply to all institutions, bodies, agencies and offices of the european union, albeit to a limited extent for the court of justice, the european central bank and the european investment bank. for citizens, the lisbon treaty will mean real progress when all eu bodies will apply a common set of rules on access to documents. such a single set of rules ensures consistency, but at the same time it must be tailored to fit the great number of bodies with very different mandates and competences. i would also like to repeat what i have said on previous occasions in this house and elsewhere. regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 is the cornerstone of a policy on transparency, but we also need to think about what we can do proactively outside the formal legislation. that is why i announced at the joint committee meeting of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs of 20 january that i am taking the initiative to prepare an openness action plan. improved registers, greater user-friendliness and accessibility, active dissemination, and quicker publishing of documents are some examples of what i want to address in this action plan and, of course, continue to discuss with the other eu institutions. this is a pragmatic and efficient way to mainstream transparency into all our policies. we need to lead by example. in this spirit, we should also look at ways to make our institutions and the way they operate more understandable to citizens. we need an active policy of informing citizens and making them aware of how europe-wide policies affect their everyday life. regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 is, of course, an important tool but, beyond the legal text, it is how we put this into practice that really counts. to sum up the commission’s position on mr cashman’s report at this stage of the procedure, i would like to say the following. there are some amendments the commission cannot accept because they go beyond the legal base of article 255 of the treaty. there are other amendments we cannot accept because they go beyond the scope of the commission’s proposed changes, but in some cases such amendments nevertheless point to important issues that may well be addressed in another context. also, the commission is always willing to take on board good ideas in whatever context it may be. once we have parliament’s and the council’s positions, you will have the position from the third corner in the institutional triangle. i look forward to an interesting and thought-provoking discussion to come. the subject deserves that, and our citizens are entitled to expect clear and well-functioning legislation on public access to our documents.

the next item is the debate on the proposal for a council regulation establishing a multiannual recovery plan for bluefin tuna in the eastern atlantic and the mediterranean (com (2009) 0093 - c6-0081/2009 - 2009/0029 (cns)).
member of the commission. − mr president, firstly i would like to stress the importance that the commission attaches to the sustainability of the bluefin tuna stocks and fisheries, and also the importance of the european parliament in this process. within the framework of the 2006 recovery plan for eastern bluefin tuna and on the basis of an evaluation of its implementation during the 2006, 2007 and 2008 fishing seasons and in the light of new scientific advice, iccat decided to adopt a new recovery plan. the iccat scientific committee clearly indicated its view that the 2006 recovery plan was insufficient to recover the stock and reiterated its concerns with respect to the level of tac and excess of fishing effort. furthermore, iccat contracting parties identified certain failures in the implementation of the 2006 plan and so decided to adopt a new plan. this plan addresses the concerns of the scientific committee, notably by reducing the tac level and by introducing new measures to address fishing and farming capacity. it should also be noted that, at the initiative of the european community, the new recovery plan introduced the obligation for annual fishing plans at iccat level. this is an effective instrument to avoid overfishing by identifying the vessels that are over 24 metres fishing for bluefin tuna and setting their individual quotas. i am convinced that the establishment of the annual fishing plan is a key tool in ensuring the full respect of the quota. the new recovery plan also improves the existing one and introduces new control measures to address those failures identified by the contracting parties, to which philippe morillon referred. the main measures introduced in the new recovery plan are a substantial reduction in the tac from 27 500 to 22 000 tonnes in 2009 and further reductions to 19 950 tonnes for 2010 and 18 500 tonnes in 2011. the ec quota for 2009 is thus reduced to 12 406 tonnes from the 15 641 tonnes foreseen in the 2006 plan. the fishing seasons for all years are reduced, in particular for purse seiners, which account for the bulk of this fishery. the measures to freeze and reduce fishing and farming capacity are a brand new and decisive component of the new plan. overcapacity has been identified for some time as a key driver of overfishing. now is the time to address this issue in a real manner and the community, like other iccat members, has to share in the effort to do so. the introduction of the fishing plans i have already mentioned is another measure. furthermore, the derogations to minimum size are adjusted. on the atlantic, pelagic trawlers no longer benefit from derogations, while the derogations applicable to the artisanal coastal fishery have been removed, except for one case. indeed, only bait boats still benefit from previous derogations. in the mediterranean, the artisanal coastal fishery now benefits from a derogation. the control measures are reinforced, in particular as regards joint fishing operations, the adoption of a general prohibition of transhipment at sea and the introduction of a regional iccat observer programme. in conclusion, the situation of the eastern bluefin tuna is considered to be extremely serious. the overshooting of quotas, the lack of compliance, notably as regards data collection and transmission, undermine the recovery process. however, i am confident that our agreement to urgently adopt measures to eliminate overfishing and to ensure strict compliance with iccat measures can turn around the situation and bring the bluefin tuna stock to sustainable levels. we need to ensure that situations similar to those that occurred last year do not happen again in the future. the best means to achieve this is the speedy adoption by the council of the new recovery plan for bluefin tuna. any delay in the adoption of this regulation should, therefore, be avoided, especially if we want to ensure the credibility of the community at international level and to promote the process of the recovery of this stock. i am convinced that, if this plan is fully respected, it represents a realistic chance for the gradual recovery of bluefin tuna. consequently, decisive and effective action is immediately needed at the european community level. after its adoption, the commission is resolved to work closely with the member states and with other iccat contracting parties to ensure and closely monitor the full implementation of the recovery plan. finally, i wish to express my appreciation for the constructive approach and the cooperation adopted by the european parliament in dealing with this sensitive subject, reflecting our shared interest and commitment to ensuring that the community fisheries policy and our international obligations are fully respected.
i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in the negotiations, but that it should be involved in the negotiations. but i would also like to remind you that no recovery plan is going to save bluefin tuna unless fishing capacity is reduced, starting with the capacity of some community fleets, well known and noted for years on this subject, years in which the states concerned have allowed their vessels to multiply to scandalous limits in the face of the european commission's passivity, which has brought us to this almost hopeless situation. when the current recovery plan was adopted in 2007, i tabled an amendment, accepted by this house and incorporated by the commission into its final text, to oblige member states to submit fishing plans demonstrating that the capacity of their fleet is in line with the quota allocated. however, in 2008 we had to close the fisheries again early, even earlier than the previous year, when we found that in just a few weeks almost the entire community quota had been used up, in other words we were even worse off. article 5 of the new recovery plan now obliges member states with excess capacity to eliminate at least 25% of it by 2010. not only do i find the reduction incredibly mild for the excesses committed, but in the light of the precedent i am extremely concerned about the ability of the commission and the international convention for the conservation of atlantic tunas (iccaa) to enforce this obligation in the face of the obvious lack of political will more than demonstrated by the member states involved. i therefore ask and request the commissioner to give us assurances here that this lack of political will will not be passed on to the commission and that this time the commission will act firmly, beyond a new early closure of fisheries this spring.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, the proposal for a council regulation establishing a multiannual recovery plan for bluefin tuna in the eastern atlantic and mediterranean implements the binding decision adopted by consensus by the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas (iccaa) at its annual meeting in november 2008. this regulation - as has already been said - must enter into force before the start of the fishing season in april, which means that this mandatory consultation of the european parliament is taking place in this plenary session, and we are anxious to contribute to the achievement of a political agreement in the council as soon as possible on this matter which we consider to be of the utmost importance and deserves our utmost consideration. the committee on fisheries of the european parliament therefore unanimously voted in favour of urgency. the annual fishing plans, the reduction of the fishing season, the reinforcement of the control system, the spawning areas in the mediterranean and the presence of iccat observers in the hake fisheries and tuna farms covered by the regulation are intended - and i think they will succeed - to ensure compliance with the management measures adopted and to ensure traceability at all stages. each contracting party - and i think it is important to point out this - will have to submit a fishing plan for fishing vessels and traps fishing for bluefin tuna in the eastern atlantic and the mediterranean, identifying, among other things, the authorized catching vessels over 24 metres and the measures established, in order to ensure that the individual quota is not exceeded. it is also important that the measures adopted include a reduction in the fishing season by extending the closure periods for purse seiners, longliners, live bait vessels and curry-canal vessels, pelagic trawlers and recreational fisheries. the adjustment plans for countries with excess fleets and farms for fattening bluefin tuna are also important. i have read a great deal about tuna these days, and i should like to make a few points in the short time i have left. the commission has also proposed that the fishing fleet be reduced to a minimum, and that the fishing fleet be reduced to a maximum of 100 000 tonnes. the european union, or three member states (france, spain and italy), together account for half of the world's bluefin tuna catches. it is therefore essential that the european union is able to provide the iccat with statistics of the same quality as the fisheries or the fishing effort involved, not least because statistics are essential if research is to be carried out to meet the needs or questions posed by the biology and ecology of bluefin tuna today, which are a real challenge for scientific research. if we want to save this species, we need to know it better. that is why i think that everything that concerns data collection and statistics is particularly important.
on behalf of the green group, mr president, the time has come to speak out. i think we're not looking at a recovery plan, but clearly what we might call a death certificate. the lack of political responsibility on the part of some governments and the commission, together with a certain blindness on the part of some in the sector, has led us to a scenario in which, rather than asking whether or not we can recover stocks, we have to ask ourselves when we will stop seeing and finding tuna in our seas and oceans. and i'm not talking about a decade, i'm talking about a lifetime at the most. in that context, the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas should actually be called the international commission for the catch of all tuna. governments and the commission have ignored the scientific advice that has been warning of the collapse again and again and hoping for a political reaction that has never come. the consequence of this attitude - we must not deceive ourselves - is a further step towards the abyss. at this point, i am afraid that we have few solutions left to save the tuna, but there is one we can still use: working to ensure that tuna is included in the cites convention list as an endangered species and thus, at least by prohibiting its marketing, guarantee its future.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all i would like to thank members for their comments and the points that have been raised in this debate, and also for accepting the request for urgency. as i stated at the start, the measures agreed in marrakesh need to be transposed as soon as possible in order to apply from the start of this fishing season. this year will clearly be a test the purse seine fleet, which is the one which causes most pressures on the bluefin tuna stock. in this regard, i would like to refer to the fact that last year we had agreed on a restructuring package which was triggered because of the fuel crisis and we are encouraging member states to make use of this restructuring package in order to bring about a reduction of the fleet, in particular of the purse seine fleet. we are hearing some encouraging news with regard to one particular member state, france, which is undertaking to encourage certain fishers to decommission their vessels in order to present moment engaging in discussions with the italian authorities in order to see whether they can effect something in this regard in the very short term. i need to underline the fact that last year we closed the fishery early so as not to come under any pressure from any member state or any group of member states. we closed the fishery early: immediately when, according to our own calculations, the overall community quota was exhausted. this year, also as a result of the annual fishing plans that have been agreed on the community’s insistence in marrakesh, we are prepared to close the fishery early with regard to particular member states. if the fleet of a particular member state overshoots its quota, we will not hesitate to close the fishery for that particular member state. in that way, only the fleet of that member state will suffer the consequences of its overshooting, and not the fleet of the whole community. i hope that will be enough to fine-tune our action even further during the course of the fishing season. if we do not deliver on this new recovery plan, then in the years to come we will have to face the serious consequence that the whole fishery should not open at all in the coming years. i hope that we will be able to deliver on this plan. therefore i do not agree, regrettably, with what mr romeva i rueda said that the recovery plan is a death certificate. i think that the recovery plan, if properly implemented, gives us a realistic and reasonable chance to see to it that the stock does recover. the fact that we have reduced quotas from 15 641 tonnes to 12 406 tonnes in 2009, the fact that by virtue of what we are discussing today and by virtue of the council decision that hopefully will be taken later in the month, the fact that we are going to implement the marrakesh recovery plan adopted in november, from this very fishing season, is indicative of the fact that we mean business. we are not prepared to accept any abuse of the fishing possibilities that are based on what was agreed in marrakesh. we have not waited for the natural implementation of the marrakesh agreement, which would have come too late in the fishing season for bluefin tuna; we have decided to have all the parameters of the marrakesh plan introduced from the very start. i hope that these will be properly adhered to because in that way we will be able together to recover this endemic stock. if not, however, then next year we will have to speak another language.

member of the commission. − madam president, first of all i would like to convey the apologies of my colleague, louis michel, for not being able to be here in person, as he is in the congo. however, it is with great pleasure that i will take up the points, because they are so important. the commission fully agrees that water and sanitation service provision is naturally addressed at the local level, through local government, municipalities and communities. we have to recognise, however, that weaknesses exist between those different levels, most notably in weaker countries where the provision of basic services is not a strong priority. last year, the european development days here in strasbourg focused on the role of local authorities, who are at the heart of access to essential services, as well as on the importance of local governance and the participation of citizens. this is obviously a central issue for the water sector and the commission, through its different instruments, is working to increase support to local authorities and reinforce partnerships between local actors from the north and the south. at eu level, european water policy is also based on the principle of good governance, encouraging the involvement and participation of citizens, local communities, ngos and stakeholders. this is reflected not only in the water framework directive but also in initiatives such as the eu water initiative launched at the world summit on sustainable development in johannesburg, which contains the reinforcement of the role of local actors among its objectives. in africa, where the millennium development goals linked to water and sanitation are still not on track, investments need to increase, and the commission has demonstrated its political commitment by creating a financial mechanism. the water facility of half a billion euros has enabled mobilisation of double that amount through cofinancing of a large number of programmes to improve the water, sanitation and hygiene situation of millions of people. it has also improved water governance and management in acp countries. the focus on the involvement of local actors has been one of the added values of this facility. the eu will be represented at the ministerial segment of the world water forum by the current czech presidency. the statement that is being prepared includes references to the need for good governance through capacity development and institutional reform at all levels. the commission’s policy, approved in 2002, promotes integrated water resources management in developing countries. it is in this framework that the different uses of water – such as drinking water, sanitation, irrigation etc. – have to be addressed, in order to reach an optimal allocation of benefits among all users. moreover, the best practices of different experiences of green belts around cities, particularly in africa, are currently being analysed in the context of the ‘great green wall for the sahara and the sahel’ initiative as part of a feasibility study supported by the european commission. further support to this initiative will be considered in the framework of the africa-eu partnership on climate change. i am pleased to announce that the water facility will continue under the 10th european development fund and that eur 200 million has been set aside for that purpose. member states are invited to participate with additional funding. the commission’s strategy is based on an integrated framework for collaboration with partner governments, eu member states and all the stakeholders concerned. the water facility complements the national programmes with its capacity to work with decentralised actors and develop innovative solutions. the ongoing preparation of the 10th edf water facility identifies in particular the potential offered by public water operators, who provide over 90% of water and sanitation services globally. therefore, public-public partnerships potentially constitute a very cost-effective approach in terms of promoting the relevant ‘good governance’ principle in the acp water sector, with potentially long-term and sustainable impacts on institutional and organisational change. such ‘twinning’ partnerships – for instance through training and technical assistance – can be efficient ways to promote the principles of good governance in the water sector in acp countries. finally, let me confirm that aid effectiveness and the division of labour are discussed with relevant partners within the mechanisms of the eu water initiative. a mapping of eu development assistance in the water sector has been carried out to improve that ongoing dialogue. the question of donor orphans is an important one in the water sector and the commission intends to take this into account in the conception of the new water facility under the 10th edf.
on behalf of the pse group. madam president, i am very pleased that the fifth world water forum is being held in istanbul and that the european union is also taking part, with a representative of the commission and a delegation from the european parliament. i also understand and support the need to support local public authorities in achieving democratic and participatory systems of better or innovative water management, and to support decentralisation processes as well. all this with the primary and overriding objective of defending the fundamental right to water and sanitation, but, of course, within a rigorous framework of respect for sustainable development, which in the european union is embodied in the water framework directive as a reference, and with the millennium development goals as a background in the field of development. i have to say that all this - and i will put it this way tomorrow in an amendment which i hope this house will accept - was discussed this summer at the international expo in zaragoza 2008, in which the european parliament, for the first time, also took part alongside the commission on an equal footing. more than 2000 experts, in the water tribunal, ngos, in the forum called el faro, as well as delegations from the commission and parliament, discussed and generated a huge pool of discussion and very interesting and creative proposals on water management. this was perpetuated in a charter of zaragoza 2008, adopted on 14 september 2008, with 17 points, some of which i would like to highlight. it says: that access to safe drinking water and sanitation is a human right that must be guaranteed by public authorities; that access to water is a powerful driver of development; that predictions indicate that climate change is capable of changing water availability and needs across the planet; that the sustainability of food production is directly linked to the efficient use of water. that the watershed unit is the most efficient territorial area for water use and the best place to resolve conflicts between countries, regions or users; and finally, that public intervention should take the initiative to promote appropriate legislation and structuring of water rights. i would ask the commissioner to take account of the conclusions of this 'zaragoza charter', which was drawn up with the participation of experts, ngos, associations, the commission and parliament, and which really served as a forum for debate prior to the fifth world water forum in istanbul. i think it is worthwhile to integrate the conclusions of this charter and also of the water tribunal into the european discussion and debate that we are presenting as the european union in the pavilion at this international exhibition.

the rapporteur. - mr president, latin america is a continent of over 600 million people, contributing more than 10% of the world's gross domestic product, with 40% of the world's plant species and, at the same time, a young, dynamic and extraordinarily active capital. however, despite the economic boom of recent years, latin america is not in the best moment from the point of view of its integration. president óscar arias said this at his inauguration and we recalled this this weekend at a seminar organized in são paulo with the former president of peru, alejandro toledo, and the former president of brazil, fernando enrique cardoso. there have been tensions between argentina and uruguay, the alca project has failed, venezuela has left the andean community, there have been problems between brazil and bolivia over the nationalisation of energy resources, between argentina and bolivia for the same reason, between ecuador and colombia, between colombia and venezuela, between mexico and venezuela, etc. the european commission's initiative, supported by parliament and the council, to establish this strategic partnership is therefore a clear and well-defined message that latin america remains on the agenda of the priorities for action by the european union, thanks in part to the personal commitment of commissioner ferrero-waldner. in the case of mexico, this strategic partnership particularly wants to underline the importance of this country in latin american and world forums and, moreover, is a key and essential step to consolidate existing relations with mexico and to expand coordination on issues of global importance. this new step is an opportunity to further strengthen political dialogue and coordinate the positions of both sides at the global level, as well as the various multilateral forums and international institutions, through consultation mechanisms that allow joint positions to be adopted on specific issues of global scope such as security, the environment or socioeconomic issues. for the european union, it is also an excellent opportunity to have a privileged relationship with a country which occupies a leading position in latin american forums, such as the rio group, where it holds the presidency until 2010, and which is part of the g-20, the g8+5, the world trade organisation, the international monetary fund and also the oecd, being the only latin american country to be present in this body. so finding common solutions to the global economic and financial crisis, developing ambitious strategies for the success of the un climate change conference in copenhagen, developing a structured dialogue on immigration or working together to achieve the millennium development goals are some of the things that the annual summits between the european union and mexico can achieve, if this strategic partnership is enabled as we are proposing. parliament too, in the resolution it will adopt this morning, will once again reiterate its support for president calderón in the fight against drug trafficking and organised crime; and i believe that we must also, from a position of respect, dialogue and shared responsibility, take on common challenges, such as the fight against vulnerable sectors of society, such as women or representatives of the media. commissioner, this year we are celebrating the 25th anniversary of the san josé political dialogue, in which, thanks to a large mobilization of central american political talent and the support of the european union, it was possible to pacify the central american isthmus, which was ravaged by civil conflicts. i believe that support for peace, understanding, harmony and reconciliation is an honourable task which the european union has been carrying out in central america and elsewhere. now that these values are being consolidated, not without difficulty and not everywhere equally, the time for development is clearly ringing in, which, without integration, from our european experience, will be more difficult. i believe that with this strategic partnership with mexico we are giving a great boost and above all we are sending a clear and well-defined signal of europe's commitment to latin america.

over others. it is basically a legal necessity, derived from the very rules of legality established by the world trade organization. it is a necessity arising from the situation in which our previous trade legal framework with the acp countries found itself. and it should be remembered, also in this house and at this time, that those who denounced the european union's relations with the acp countries were precisely other developing countries, which had perfectly legitimate demands for access to our markets, but which, by the mere fact of not being former colonies of countries which are now members of the european union, had been left out. the european union therefore had, and still has, two standards: one for its former colonies and another for other countries with a similar level of development that do not have such a system. that is what was becoming unsustainable and what those same countries, in the world trade organization, were busy stressing. on the other hand, we must remember another truth: the system we are going to replace, first lomé, then the system derived from the cotonou agreements, has never produced the expected results. no one can claim that the cotonou system was perfectly satisfactory. if it were, the figures for the volume of trade of the european union with these countries would be much higher than we have today. so let's not presume that we're mr president, in december 2007, the heads of state and government of the european union approved in lisbon the joint africa-european union strategy and the first action plan for its implementation. the strategy was motivated by three realities. the first is the coexistence on the african continent of peace processes and the progressive consolidation of democratic systems, with persistent conflicts, such as that in darfur, high rates of poverty and the emergence of phenomena such as the mass flows of illegal immigration. the second of the realities is that sub-saharan africa is the poorest region on the planet. a population with low life expectancy, low levels of schooling and literacy and high population growth. 300 million people survive on less than a euro a day. the third reality is that africa is the physical setting for the major pandemics, the place where more than two-thirds of the people who are infected with aids live and where 90 percent of the deaths caused by malaria occur. this year we have made little progress on the objectives we set ourselves then, and since the action plan covers until 2010, there is a need for urgent action in two major areas: cooperation on democratic governance, institutional strengthening and strengthening the role of civil society, with particular attention to gender policies, and cooperation to achieve the coverage of basic social needs, the fight against hunger and the launching of development policies in the areas of education, health and access to basic goods such as water.
