the rapporteur. - mr president, first of all i would like to thank the alternative rapporteurs, in particular mr severin, mr lambsdorff and mr lagendijk, and also the committee on foreign affairs and the authors of the opinions, mr garcía-margallo and mrs quisthoudt-rowohl. i thank everyone for their cooperation in the preparation of this report on relations between the european union and the united states. we have thus obtained a report on an important matter with broad consensus. the report we are voting on tomorrow is therefore a strong and decisive message from the european parliament at a very opportune moment. and i say this as an important matter because it is clear that the european union and the united states are two very important actors in the world, who must work closely together, as befits those who share the same principles and values, and many interests. the report's main thrust is that we are at a very opportune moment to strengthen the transatlantic relationship. and this is basically for three reasons. the first is a new, pragmatic administration in the united states, which knows that no country can face global challenges alone and which has aroused great expectations in european and world public opinion. the second is a stronger european union, more capable of acting abroad than the union of 1995, when the new transatlantic agenda was agreed; moreover, it will soon be a union strengthened by the instruments of foreign and defence policy of the lisbon treaty. and the third, a new context, marked by global challenges like the economic crisis or climate change, and no longer just military challenges, as in the past. for the new challenges, cooperation with the european union will be very useful to the united states. this transatlantic relationship must be strengthened on two levels: an institutional level and a material level, of practical cooperation. we must take advantage of the lisbon treaty to strengthen institutional structures; two annual summits, not just one, attended by the new permanent president of the european council; also, create a transatlantic political council, which meets quarterly with the high representative - and vice-president of the commission - and the secretary of state; raise the level of dialogue between legislators by creating a transatlantic assembly and also improve the transatlantic economic council. all these improvements will make coordination more intensive and effective; they should be incorporated in a new transatlantic association agreement, and negotiations should start when the lisbon treaty enters into force. the other objective of the report is to strengthen cooperation in practice. it is about setting an agenda for jointly tackling numerous challenges and conflicts, as well as bilateral issues. to achieve this common agenda, the council and the commission must intensify their contacts with the new government in washington in the coming months. i therefore welcome the summit with president obama in prague on 5 april, as stated in the amendment tabled by my group. the report identifies a number of global challenges on which the united states and the european union should seek common approaches, such as the economic crisis, effective multilateralism that integrates emerging actors, the millennium development goals, climate change, the promotion of human rights, etc. it also deals with a number of regional issues where we must act in a coordinated way. these are conflicts such as the middle east, the iranian nuclear programme and afghanistan; relations with russia and the countries of latin america are also mentioned. disarmament and security issues are areas where better coordination is also needed, including the fight against the grave threat of terrorism, which must be carried out in full respect of international law and human rights. the report also deals with certain bilateral issues in the fields of justice and home affairs, including the issue of visas. it also stressed the need for the transatlantic partnership to enjoy broad support from civil society, especially young people. economic and trade relations are also included in the report, which stresses the need to move forward with the integration of the transatlantic market. and in these matters, of course, i have incorporated many suggestions from the economic and foreign trade committees. and, ladies and gentlemen, i'm through with you. with this report, i believe that parliament will send a clear message tomorrow, if it is adopted. we call for a strengthening of eu-us relations, including at the institutional level. i believe that this strengthening will benefit both sides and also the entire international community.

informal meeting with president obama, namely: firstly, energy security and climate change; secondly, economic cooperation; and, thirdly, cooperation on security and external relations. i listened carefully to other comments made, such as the need to build a new transatlantic agenda, to deepen cooperation in foreign assistance and development policy, to pursue cooperation in justice and home affairs, to keep up the momentum on the transatlantic economic council, to explore setting up the transatlantic political council etc. we will take them into account as we prepare for the regular eu-us summit to be held in june. those of you who raised the other issues, such as the visa waiver – because not all the eu countries are taking part in that – can remember how, a year ago, my country led efforts on that. it was also the subject of a debate in this parliament, so i can assure you that we will continue to raise this issue with the us government as well. in conclusion, i would like to add the following reflections. it seems clear that the new us administration has taken on board many of the messages that we have been sending them over recent months and years about the transatlantic relationship. they are now responding. for example, we are now being asked to provide greater strategic input on afghanistan. it is also clear that strategic input is expected to be matched by a very practical commitment, so i believe that you will remember this when we are discussing our practical contribution to the future afghan mission. it should come as no surprise for us once we are really engaged in a deep and serious debate. when president obama said in berlin last year that america has no better partner than europe, he was not just making a statement of principle, but also inviting europe to provide the proof. secondly, it is clear to all of us that the challenges we are facing are getting more numerous and more complex. to return to one of my opening points, when the eu and the us agree, we can help set the global agenda. that also means taking our share of leadership and leading others to lend their support and provide means towards the goals set. but to be able to do so and be a credible partner to the us, the eu must speak with one voice to the greatest extent possible. the czech presidency will continue to ensure that the transatlantic partnership remains one of the cornerstones of the eu’s foreign policy. i look forward to developing this relationship further as we face new challenges together and i look forward to continued cooperation with this parliament in doing so.
member of the commission. − mr president, as many have said, this debate has shown that it is a question of how we can implement the most important issues together with such a crucial strategic partner as the united states of america. since i made quite a number of very clear and practical remarks at the beginning, i will just make a few concrete remarks now. first, the role of legislators in, and the institutional set-up of, eu-us relations is very important. in principle, we unequivocally support stronger links between the eu and us legislators. obviously, the primary impetus for this must come from the law-makers themselves. i know that the european parliament is ready to do so, and this should also come from congress. nevertheless, i suggest that it would be worthwhile for eu legislators also to cultivate more intensive contacts with the senate, which has a longer electoral cycle, and with congressmen whose sectoral expertise could advance the agenda of the transatlantic economic council. the lisbon treaty, as and when it enters into force, will then, as has been said, also give the ep a reinforced role in shaping eu-us dialogue, especially on regulatory matters; as has been mentioned, think-tanks will certainly also be very important not only from the us side to us but also from the eu side to the us. concerning eu-us institutions, i would caution, first, that the transatlantic agenda should be driven by substance rather than by process. in our first meetings with president obama, therefore, as i have said before, it will be important to demonstrate the capacity to focus on results. however, i have taken careful note of your call for an overhaul of the current arrangements under the new transatlantic agenda. i intend to initiate a review of the structures to help them deliver better, and the commission will come up with due proposals. let me also speak briefly on the transatlantic economic council (tec). mr verheugen has already had a meeting with his new us counterpart, mr froman, on 23 march 2009. the main issues of the tec under the new administration are as follows. firstly, raising the profile of political strategic issues, while at the same time relieving the burden of more technical matters on the summit agendas. secondly, the time horizon for a future work programme – here mr verheugen wants to set a very long-term perspective, but this has to be weighed against the mandate of this commission and we need to have some short-term results. finally, how to deal with pressure from the member states – to whom we have promised, but not yet delivered, a mid-term programme – to be more involved in the work of the tec. second, i would like to point out that we are a community which shares values with the us, but there are still things that have to be done. therefore we will need to continue to encourage the us to sign up to core un human rights conventions, including those on discrimination against women, and the rights of the child – to name but a few. this includes our position on the icc, as has been stressed on several occasions with the bush administration, but that will be taken up again. third, concerning visa waiver and visa reciprocity, which many of you mentioned: we know that, owing to substantive efforts by member states and at eu level, seven member states were admitted to the visa-waiver programme in november/december 2008. however, there are still five member states which do not yet enjoy visa-free travel to the us. we will, therefore, continue to raise this issue. i can tell you that vice-president barrot and the czech minister langer raised the issue again last week in washington and the us side has generally shown understanding of our position, while stressing at the same time that the action of the federal government is based on statutory requirements, which clearly set the framework of future enlargements of the programme and are being monitored closely by congress. secretary napolitano informed us that one additional member state is getting very close to entering the visa-waiver programme. finally, concerning afghanistan: not only have we already delivered a lot in the past, but, as i have said before, we are ready to contribute to the civilian search, and there will be some additional funding that we will find from our asia budget for the elections, the police and, most probably, for agriculture because it is important to have additional alternative livelihoods. i am always open to new ideas, and one example, which is taken up in your report, would be to upgrade the foreign ministers’ meetings into a transatlantic political council with a heavier focus on strategic themes. as i have said before, we intend to look at revamping the existing transatlantic agenda in that perspective, against the background of the 15th anniversary of the new transatlantic agreement in 2010.
the rapporteur. - mr president, first of all i would like to thank you for the speeches and the congratulations. what i think is most important about this debate is that there is a broad consensus on the importance of the eu-us relationship and also on the need to strengthen it, not only through a joint agenda to deal with serious challenges and serious conflicts, but also through new institutional mechanisms. with a few exceptions, i have not seen any major objections to either the two annual summits, or the establishment of a transatlantic political council, or, of course, to the improvement or raising of the level of the dialogue of legislators to a more strengthened dialogue, to a kind of transatlantic assembly, as the report advocates. i am also pleased that the commissioner has found this strengthening of the dialogue between legislators very useful and that neither she nor the council representative is opposed to this other strengthening of other institutions, which i believe is largely required by the treaty of lisbon. this will be very timely and beneficial for both parties. i cannot respond in one minute to all the comments i have heard, but i do want to say, on russia, that as mr severin knows, the report advocates constructive cooperation, without prejudice, of course, to human rights and international law; president-in-office of the council. − mr president, i certainly welcome the interest of members of parliament in the issue of the eu’s relationship with turkmenistan, and i am pleased to have the opportunity to respond on behalf of the council to the various questions and issues which have been raised in parliament. turkmenistan is in many ways growing in importance. for a long time it has been a very inward-looking country. but, over the last two years, it has taken a number of significant steps to open up to the outside world. the government is increasingly open to cooperation. this is reflected in a greater effort to work more constructively within the framework of the eu’s central asian strategy. despite these changes, our contractual relationship with turkmenistan has remained unchanged for 20 years. as mr wiersma stated, it is still based on the outdated trade and commercial and economic cooperation agreement with the soviet union. against the background of positive developments in turkmenistan, we have an opportunity to strengthen our bilateral relationship. the interim agreement, which was signed in 1999, provisionally applies the trade-related parts of the partnership and cooperation agreement, also signed in 1999, for which only three member state ratifications remain outstanding. there are many aspects to the union’s relations with turkmenistan. the promotion of human rights and democracy is, of course, at the heart of the bilateral relationship, as it is key to the wider strategy for central asia. the fact that turkmenistan borders afghanistan makes it also a strategically important country. at the same time, turkmenistan is participating in the reconstruction of afghanistan and provides logistics background for operations or activities of many eu member states in the framework of the isaf (overflights) as well as on a bilateral basis. turkmenistan is critical to regional security and the fight against drug trafficking. its growing economy provides opportunities for eu companies. in addition, turkmenistan is a key partner in the diversification of the eu’s energy relations and energy security. these are all important areas which we need to develop in our own interests. in addition, since the presidential elections in february 2007, turkmenistan has engaged in a number of significant reforms, including constitutional changes. many of the new provisions in the constitution, as well as other reforms which have been announced, underline that the country is moving in the right direction, even though it is a long-term process and much more still needs to be done. on the question of human rights, turkmenistan has engaged constructively in a human rights dialogue with the eu on a wide range of issues. this dialogue has also been matched by some important developments within the country. in particular, some political prisoners have been released, and there has been increased cooperation with the un. turkmenistan has also permitted the un rapporteur on freedom of religion to visit, it has participated fully in the un periodic review, and a un centre for preventive diplomacy has been established in ashgabat. in addition, internal travel restrictions have been eased, a dialogue with the icrc has begun, and education reform has restored ten-year secondary and five-year university-level education. turkmenistan has acceded to international conventions such as the second optional protocol to the international covenant on civil and political rights and the convention on the political rights of women. all this is evidence that turkmenistan is moving ahead. of course, much remains to be done in the field of human rights and respect for the rule of law and democracy. we will continue to push in particular for the release of all political prisoners, for free access by the icrc to prisoners, for a lifting of the restrictions on foreign travel, and for freedom for the media and civil society. the presidency is convinced that the best way to ensure that turkmenistan delivers on these issues is through constant engagement. we have to be able to have an open dialogue, and, when necessary, send clear messages, if turkmenistan is to move towards full respect for international standards. this is precisely why we need to upgrade our relationship and our own instruments and tools. the current contractual arrangement with turkmenistan provides for only a rudimentary bilateral dialogue. the only treaty-based dialogue consists of a meeting of a joint committee at officials level once a year. the interim agreement would make human rights an essential element of relations, and would therefore strengthen our ability to influence future developments in turkmenistan in this area. the pca, once in force, would go further by providing for a fully-fledged political dialogue. the eu strategy for central asia, adopted in june 2007, states that, ‘in order to intensify cooperation with central asian states, the eu will make full use of the potential of partnership and cooperation agreements’. such agreements already exist in the case of kazakhstan, kyrgyzstan and uzbekistan. and in the case of tajikistan, an interim agreement is in force pending the ratification and entry into force of the pca. for the successful implementation of the eu strategy for central asia it is important to have all central asian countries involved, and that is why it is important to create conditions for involvement of turkmenistan as well. without it the implementation of our goals and interests in central asia would be very difficult. the presidency is convinced that we need now to establish an appropriate legal framework for our relations with turkmenistan, beginning with the interim agreement. this will enable us to build on the developments taking place in the country, and to strengthen our wider engagement with central asia. the interim agreement is the most effective way of ensuring that turkmenistan makes progress in the various key areas which i have outlined, not least in respect for human rights, democracy and the rule of law. i know that you share these objectives, and therefore hope that we can count on your support for taking this forward.
member of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, since the election of president berdimukhamedov, turkmenistan has indeed entered a new phase of its development, and several positive signs of change have emerged. the new leaders are more open-minded. for example, they lifted some restrictions on freedom of movement within the country, amended the constitution to strengthen the role of parliament, created an institute for democracy and human rights, hosted the un centre for preventive diplomacy in ashgabat, and for the first time allowed international observers to attend the parliamentary elections last december. furthermore, as you know, reforms in the education and health sectors are now a priority for the government. in 2006, the european parliament proposed to the turkmen authorities a number of measures to enable it to finally deliver a favourable opinion on the interim trade agreement. and in the last two years, since the election of the new president, many of the measures proposed have been adopted - i do not want to repeat those mentioned by the president of the council, particularly concerning the icrc. reforms have also been initiated in the field of education, with the modernisation of the education system, teacher training abroad, the extension of schooling and the introduction of the internet in schools. a few prisoners have been released, including recently my dear colleague in parliament, mr valery pal, whose release we had called for. and in september 2008, for the first time ever, a visit was granted to the un special rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief, who concluded that, and i quote, "although some religious individuals and communities still face difficulties, the situation has improved significantly since 2007". the launch of new structured dialogues, as we have heard, on human rights is another positive point. of course, you can be sure that in these meetings we will always address topics of concern, including the situation of political prisoners, freedom of assembly, media, worship, minority rights, and we will emphasize at every opportunity our commitment to respect for human rights and their importance for long-term economic and social development. because of these concerns, which are certainly legitimate, about the situation in turkmenistan, parliament postponed its decision on the interim agreement. i share some of the fears in principle and i also recognize that turkmenistan still has a long way to go before it achieves full respect for international standards of democracy and human rights. however, even if it is limited, it is a positive development, showing a willingness to move forward and to be open to change. we see it as an opportunity to engage with and encourage the turkmen authorities. i am firmly convinced that the european union must do more to work towards positive developments. the application of the interim trade agreement, i.e. the trade provisions of the partnership and cooperation agreement, would be a positive first step which would allow us to engage more with turkmenistan and to promote more vigorously cooperation, reform and modernisation as a whole, and the interim agreement contains a key human rights clause and i am aware of your concerns about the possibility of suspending the agreement. in this connection, i would like to point out that the interim trade agreement, in article 1, and the partnership and cooperation agreement, in article 2, contain clauses referring to respect for democracy and fundamental rights as essential elements of each agreement, but above all that both agreements contain clauses allowing each party to take appropriate measures in the event of a serious breach of their terms, even without consulting the joint committees in the event of a particular emergency. the suspension of agreements in the event of an established, continuous and serious violation of the human rights clause is therefore possible. but it is clear that the interim trade agreement is not the panacea. it will certainly not solve all human rights problems in turkmenistan; however, it will contribute to greater adherence to international standards, in particular in the area of the rule of law and human rights. we have two further important reasons for strengthening our relations with turkmenistan to protect our own interests: security and energy. the fact is that turkmenistan is located at the crossroads of europe and asia and neighbours, for example, iran and afghanistan, and its active neutrality is important in a region of high tension which is conducive to destabilisation. to this end, we are successfully cooperating with turkmenistan in the field of border management and in the fight against terrorism, islamic extremism, drug trafficking and human trafficking. this cooperation is all the more important in view of the recent renewed engagement of the international community in afghanistan and pakistan and the forthcoming regional conferences in the hague and tokyo. as we all know, central asia could play a very important role in energy security. since the change of regime in turkmenistan, we have strengthened our cooperation in this area. the european union is making every effort to complete the southern european gas corridor as part of a wider policy of diversifying energy sources and transit routes. clearly, turkmenistan is essential to the success of this project. in conclusion, our relations with turkmenistan must be shaped by both our values and our interests. that is why i remain convinced that by engaging with turkmenistan we will be in a better position to make our case for a more open society in that country. we will continue to urge the authorities to move forward in other areas, such as reform of the criminal and civil code and legislation on religion, freedom of the media, release of political prisoners, allowing international observers access to prisons and increased registration of ngos in the country. for all these reasons, i would ask you to support the favourable opinion on the interim agreement with turkmenistan.

member of the commission. − mr president, first of all i would like to thank parliament for the very strong interest it has expressed and its continuous involvement with regard to ship dismantling. i would especially like to thank mr blokland. this is a very good starting point for further action at eu level to ensure that the european union plays its part in solving this international problem. these questions are also timely, in the light of the recent ruling of the bangladeshi high court that you have just mentioned and the situation in that country. as a consequence of this ruling, all ship recycling yards will be closed within two weeks as they have not been authorised by the ministry of the environment. the import of dangerous ships that are on a list will be banned and all imported ships will have to be pre-cleaned. finally, bangladesh will start developing a national law on ship breaking in line with the basel convention. now, let me turn to the situation closer to home by answering your questions. your first question concerns the phasing-out of the beaching method – the method of dismantling end-of-life vessels directly on the beach. i share your concerns about the serious risks this presents to human health and the environment. we considered the question of introducing an eu ban on beaching in the impact assessment of our strategy. there were some concerns regarding the effectiveness of any such ban since it would be only applicable to eu-flagged ships and could be easily and legally circumvented by changing flag. we believe it will be more effective to put our efforts into ensuring that the technical guidelines currently being developed to support the future imo convention really do lead to safe and environmentally sound ship recycling. the progress in the development of these guidelines is, so far, very encouraging. it is very doubtful in any case that the traditional beaching method would be able to comply with the forthcoming guidelines. and, regarding your second question, i am pleased to confirm that the commission is fully committed to working towards an effective and early transposition of the ship recycling convention into eu legislation. the environment dg has already launched several studies and is working on assessing the impacts of the key elements of the convention. i believe that it is extremely important for the european union to show leadership and the high priority that we attach to this issue. this will encourage the ratification by third countries and consequently speed up the entry into force of this convention. but i share the concerns highlighted in your third question regarding the importance of not undermining the existing community acquis. we need to safeguard the existing requirements in terms of workers’ rights and environmental protection when transposing the imo convention. and in our study, we will therefore carefully compare the requirements of the imo convention with our community acquis. and i would like to stress that we will, in particular, ensure that the 2006 waste shipment regulation is not undermined.
i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has already taken a decision on the matter. i would therefore like to congratulate mr blokland, not only on the question but also on the resolution he has prepared. in the people's party we are in favour of fighting against the bad practices and methods used to scrap ships and therefore support mr blokland's motion for a resolution; however, there are some points which concern us. the first is paragraph 3 - which he has already mentioned - which says that ships, as a whole, must be considered as hazardous waste and, as a result, must fall within the scope of the basle convention. we have tabled an amendment on this point because there are different interpretations within and outside the european union, and we believe that the basle convention should be taken into account and not contradicted, but that the details of its application should be defined by the future international agreement on ship scrapping. the motion for a resolution also calls, in paragraph 14, for a financing mechanism based on compulsory contributions from the shipping sector. it is a bit hasty to talk about compulsory contributions at the moment, when the system for financing them has not yet been decided at the imo, and i do not think the european commission has a clear answer to this question either. finally, in paragraph 15, the commission is called upon to make clear that the state with jurisdiction over waste is the responsible state. we do not think that it is the commission's responsibility to decide this, but we think that it should also be decided in an international convention. the important thing is to ensure consistency on the future convention on ship recycling and the basle convention on the transboundary control and disposal of hazardous waste, and all this taking into account not only the basle convention but all existing legislation.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner figel', ladies and gentlemen, this report was unanimously adopted by the committee on economic and monetary affairs. it is not only an excellent result but, given the difficulty, complexity and controversial nature of the issues it deals with, an exceptional result which should give impetus and firm grounding to the new pillar of private action which is indispensable to the effective implementation of community competition policy. it is a new step towards a more advanced and effective competition policy, more respectful of the rights of victims and more effective in holding the offender to account. i would therefore like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr lehne, who has the key responsibility for the success of this mission. the quality of their approaches, their open and dialogic spirit and their intelligence in extracting the best compromises have been key to achieving this. i would like to congratulate the rapporteurs, the alternative rapporteurs and the amendments, who have contributed so positively to the enrichment of the report. the commission's white paper on actions for damages for breach of the community competition rules responds to an express request by the european parliament in connection with the green paper resolution, the content of which it welcomes to a large extent. this is the case when, among other things, it defends the complementary nature of public and private actions, and is in favour of collective actions, although avoiding the excesses of us class actions, thus facilitating the claim for damages; when it proposes access to relevant information under judicial control, although without authorizing a fishing expedition, and when it recognizes and postulates the exercise of autonomous or monitoring actions and a voluntary compensation system. this report defends the european parliament's codecision in establishing the legal framework for the exercise of actions for damages for breach of the community competition rules. this position should not be understood as a rejection of the community competition policy as the legal basis of the legislation, but as a raising of the requirements of the ordinary procedure in this area to meet higher values recognised in the treaty. where a regulation affects in a significant way a fundamental right, such as the right of citizens to effective judicial protection, which is part of the european and member states' legal systems, the democratic principle and respect for national legal traditions, which require that such matters can be regulated only by rules of a legal nature, that is to say, with the intervention of the direct representatives of the citizens, require legislative participation by the european parliament. it also proposes a horizontal and integrated approach to address the common problems that private actions in competition law may have with other areas and thus avoid fragmentary and inconsistent treatment. the exercise of private actions can be promoted by a public actor and also through individual or collective actions. this second method can be implemented directly by the victims or indirectly through qualified bodies, designated in advance or authorized on an ad hoc basis, such as consumer and business associations. in the case of actions promoted by qualified entities, the group of victims should be defined at the time of the application, but the identification of each victim may be carried out at a later, clearly defined, time and as soon as possible, avoiding unnecessary delays and respecting existing legislation. this solution is very important for minor and scattered damage cases. the report presents, in a balanced way, the access to information necessary for the exercise of monitoring actions. the protection of trade secrets must be safeguarded, as must the effectiveness of leniency programmes, for which guidelines are required. the conditions are laid down for decisions taken by an authority in the community network of competition authorities to become binding in another member state and for the burden of proof to be reversed and the presumption of fault to be established where an infringement has been established, in full respect of the principle of culpability. the reception of the 'passing-on' defence for indirect victims and a scheme to simplify and save procedures are also noteworthy. i would also like to stress the positive interaction between public and private action, both in encouraging compensation for victims and in setting the five-year period for action. i would like to conclude by expressing my appreciation to the commission for the dialogue that has been maintained throughout this procedure and by asking the commissioner to present without delay the initiatives necessary for its further development.
member of the commission. − madam president, before going into the content of this proposal, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr siekierski, and the members of the committee on agriculture and rural development for their work on this report. i would like to start by putting today’s debate into context, because this proposal is not about paragraphs, political power or promises: it is about people. millions of europeans are hit by difficult economic times and by the rapid rise we have seen in food prices since 2007. there are more people than we realise for whom the lack of adequate food is a daily concern: 43 million europeans cannot afford a meal with meat, chicken or fish every second day. i think that is a striking figure. the programme for the most deprived targets those in our society who are in need of food aid: people who worry whether they can feed their children tomorrow; people who do not think about what they will eat that night for dinner but about whether they will have anything to eat; people who enter no restaurant but the one carrying the name of resto du cœur. with more than 13 million poor people benefiting from the programme, with 19 member states participating and with the scheme being a stable outlet for intervention products, this programme has certainly shown its value. parliament recognised this already in 2006, when it called on the council and the commission to place the programme on a permanent footing for the future and to extend the distribution of foodstuffs, without restricting it to the products for which intervention applies. i am pleased to note that the report by mr siekierski endorses the commission’s approach and agrees that it is necessary to keep the programme within the common agricultural policy. this is particularly important at a time when some claim that feeding people has nothing to do with our agriculture policy. until now, the programme has been financed exclusively by the community budget. our proposal now includes cofinancing. that is a significant change, but i believe it is a fundamental improvement of the scheme. cofinancing will enable the total funds available for this measure to be more in balance with the real needs; it will encourage member states to take greater responsibility for the programme’s management, and it is also a way to strengthen the cohesive element, since cohesion countries will have less cofinancing. at the same time, i share the view that we should not run the risk of member states withdrawing from the scheme. therefore, we proposed a gradual phasing-in of cofinancing rates in order to maintain the difference between the cohesion and non-cohesion member states. i agree that we should do more to guarantee the nutritional quality of the food distributed. as the rapporteur mentioned, this could mean including fresh produce, in most cases produced locally. but it is not appropriate to outlaw foreign products or products coming from outside the european union, as proposed in your report. that would mean additional and burdensome controls. it could be seen as a signal of eu protectionism, and it could even be questioned by our wto partners. that being said, the large majority of the food distributed will in reality be produced in the european union, mainly from intervention stocks and most probably from the tenders that we are now making, in particular in the dairy sector. given that charities are heavily involved in the scheme, our proposal gives the possibility to reimburse the transport and administrative costs of the ngos. you suggest that storage costs should be covered as well. i am fundamentally in favour of this idea, but i cannot agree to your suggestion of leaving it to the member states to fix the rates of reimbursement. we need to set the same maximum rate for all participating countries, not least to make sure that the programme remains efficient and keeps the focus on supplying food. finally, let me stress that the council is waiting for the outcome of today’s debate and vote before continuing its discussions. i hope ministers have used the waiting time constructively. and from today’s debate should, therefore, be sent a clear message: do not forget those waiting in line at the soup kitchen or waiting for the next food package. so do not wait too long! we need to put this food aid scheme on a permanent footing for the future.
opinion of the committee on regional development - madam president, the economic crisis in europe will lead to an increase in the number of people below the poverty line in the coming years. that number is now 80 million, or 16 percent of the world's population. in a crisis scenario, it is essential to ensure the continuity of food supply to those most in need. with the gradual elimination of intervention stocks, an instrument which has hitherto been very useful for the supply of food to the poorest in the community is also disappearing, while at the same time ensuring stability in the prices received by european producers. it would be desirable if the new programme of aid to the poorest also served to give a start to community production. in this way we would be contributing to the maintenance of farmers within rural areas. the european commission proposal does not require the food to be included in the programme to be of exclusively community origin, as it considers that this would be contrary to the rules of the world trade organisation, but i would like to remind the commission that a country like the united states devotes no more and no less than 67% of the budget in its agricultural law to nutrition programmes for the most disadvantaged people, and also serves as a complement to aid for its farmers and cattle farmers in particular. this is in contrast to the cost of the new community programme, which would be only 1% of the cap budget.
on behalf of the pse group. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, with whom we have a great deal in common on this programme, and congratulate us all, because in times of economic crisis it is essential to maintain a programme like this, with clear positive social effects. although we are facing a consultation procedure, we must send a clear political signal from the european parliament, in these times of economic uncertainty, from brussels and strasbourg, that we are not exclusively or only concerned about a recovery of the financial system, but that we are fully aware that social policies, especially those which support those who need it most, the poorest in the european union, have to grow. this food distribution programme must continue to be considered part of the common agricultural policy - and we agree with the commission on this - not only because european agriculture has a strong social dimension, but also because it is a functioning instrument, because it is needed now more than ever and because it must continue to function. the socialist group, like the rapporteur, is against the cofinancing of this programme by the european union and the member states, since this would mean discrimination between countries on the basis of their wealth and the programme might not be able to be implemented in the countries most in need. it is not understandable that now, when we need it most, the commission wants to save community money on the more social side of the cap, especially when we take into account that there are budgetary surpluses in the agricultural budget every year. full community funding is essential for us. we need to make sure that this programme reaches all countries and especially the most needy. the 43 million potential beneficiaries of this programme are asking us to make a greater effort and in no case to save budgetary expenditure. austerity, yes; madam president, i would first of all like to congratulate mr siekierski because i think this is an excellent report, which has received a lot of support in the committee on agriculture. for more than 20 years it has been said that the community's intervention stocks have been used to provide food aid to those most in need. the problem, mr stevenson, is that successive reforms of the cap have reduced these interventions to the limit. but i also want to say here that it would be a very bad signal if we were to abolish or attempt to abolish this programme at this very delicate time when many europeans and many european women do not have enough to eat. and it is clear in this sense that when stocks do not arrive - because i have already said that they have been disappearing - we will have to resort to the market. i would like to highlight as positive elements the obligation in the report that, when products are used on the market, they must be community, fresh and of local origin. i also think that 100% community funding is appropriate, because i believe that at the moment this aid should not and cannot depend on the possibilities of each member state, unless we want to look more closely at the possibilities. i also think it is right that the programme should be extended to three years. i would simply point out that the commission is always in time to implement intervention wherever it is necessary or possible and that more than one agricultural sector would appreciate it. i am thinking of the milk producers in my region of galicia, who would benefit from the intervention to help them overcome their difficult situation and at the same time help to provide food for the most deprived.

the next item is the commission statement on collective redress.
mr president, in a market without frontiers such as the european one, it is important that, in addition to ensuring the proper functioning of competition, we should be equally concerned with consumer protection. over the past half century, barriers to products have been falling, but, to a large extent, these barriers remain for consumers. abusive commercial practices are often not reported by consumers or pursued by consumer organisations because of the awareness of the difficulty of obtaining compensation. the collective action allows for joint efforts in cases where there are many parties involved and offers a much greater prospect of achieving redress. the cross-border nature of many economic transactions in the european union means that this right to collective redress cannot be confined to national areas. we need a genuine european initiative, which will require a certain degree of harmonisation or approximation between the existing national systems to be effective. the model to be chosen should aim to facilitate access to the system for consumers, avoid excessive burdens and bureaucratization. i therefore believe that preference should be given to alternative dispute resolution mechanisms, which are the most flexible, and to simplified judicial procedures with reduced costs.
member of the commission. − mr president, i should like to thank you for all your valuable opinions. in a way, i am familiar with most of them because we have been discussing, point by point, the most important parts of your concerns and hopes for having collective redress in europe. i should like to reiterate once again that i am totally with you in not wanting us-style class actions to be introduced into european culture. i know that is one of your most important preoccupations. as ms mccarthy also mentioned, this is about damages. this is already happening in the uk, but this has nothing to do with what we are discussing and what i am proposing as our future steps in this direction. in this respect, i would like to stress the following. checking to see whether there is a real need for collective redress: yes, we are doing that and we will continue to do so after the green paper. respecting constitutional constraints: yes. avoiding us-style class action: yes. ensuring that damages are compensated, including all costs incurred by the consumer but, at the same time, excluding any element of punitive damage: yes, that is what we have in mind. discouraging unmeritorious claims, as referred to by mr rack: yes. promoting alternative dispute resolution schemes: of course, because this is less time-consuming, more affordable and easier for both consumers and businesses, and also respecting subsidiarity. with these few words, i would like to say that we are fully aware of the challenges and we are ready to face these challenges and make a good proposal, step by step, building consensus and common understanding with you. what i really appreciate today is that all of us recognise that we have a problem and that we are ready to address this problem. so this really is a very good starting point for the next stage of debates. as this is a challenge we face, i would like in particular to stress what mr lehne referred to – the common approach, the horizontal approach with commissioner kroes. commissioner kroes and myself, as well as our respective services, are cooperating very closely in order to ensure that our initiatives are consistent and produce synergies. the consistency principle does not necessarily rule out that specific situations require specific solutions. each of the two initiatives has a distinct focus. whereas the consumer green paper deals with redress for breaches of consumer protection law, the competition white paper is strictly about competition law infringements. another major difference between the two initiatives is that, whereas the consumer green paper only covers redress for consumers, the redress mechanism suggested in the competition white paper is designed to benefit both consumers and businesses. so my challenge is to achieve effective redress for our consumers and thereby restore their confidence in the market. from previous discussions, i know that the european parliament is supporting us in our efforts to achieve this goal. let me stress again that parliament, together with member states and stakeholders, will be convinced that not only is there a problem but also that an effective and balanced solution must and can be found at european level. i should like to thank you for this fruitful debate and your valuable opinions, and i look forward to working with you on this file over the coming months.

certainly know, the council discussed the relationship with russia in depth some time ago, when we established the grounds and the rationale for the new eu-russia agreement, and thus we consider it important that the negotiations for the new agreement are back on track. after all, russia is our biggest neighbour, one of our key partners and an indispensable player on the international scene. nowadays, when the economic crisis is hitting both of us equally hard, it is clear that confrontations will make neither of us any stronger. constructive, rational and mutually beneficial cooperation and fulfilment of international commitments by russia, on the other hand, certainly could. moreover, a dialogue and a constructive engagement are important means of defending our interests and promoting our values vis-à-vis russia. this, in a nutshell, provided the main impetus for our decision to resume the negotiations on the new eu-russia agreement, despite what happened in georgia last august. the crisis and its implications continue, certainly, to overshadow our relations. the negotiations in no way legitimise russia’s conduct in georgia, including in the territories of abkhazia presidency also plays a role in the negotiations. it is of the utmost importance that the new agreement should contain provision to ensure effective dialogue and cooperation with russia, and should be based on common values, compliance with the existing international commitments, the rule of law and respect for democracy, human rights and fundamental freedoms. this is particularly important in relation to our common neighbourhood. indeed, it is essential if we are to see a solution to long-standing conflicts. conflict prevention is also an important objective. it needs to be pursued through both political dialogue and joint initiatives. there is already some movement with russia on the scope of the political dialogue and external security part of the new agreement. but of course the devil is in the detail. the most interesting and challenging part of the negotiations is now beginning, as we begin to discuss concrete text proposals. given that negotiations are ongoing, it would not be appropriate to give you the details here. i can, however, assure you that we will seek to obtain substantial provisions on strengthening dialogue on the international scene, on the fight against terrorism, on arms control, disarmament and non-proliferation, on human rights, democracy and the rule of law, on crisis management and on civil protection. it was agreed at the eu-russia the arctic region is one of the most fragile regions on our planet. the consequences of unrestricted exploitation of their natural resources would be catastrophic not only for the immediate environment and the indigenous population, but for the world as a whole. the melting of large areas has brought these risks to the fore, making a new global regulation to protect the arctic, similar to the one already in place for the antarctic, necessary, even taking into account the differences already highlighted in the debate. an international treaty is needed between all the parties involved, including, no doubt, the european union, to protect its unique environment, to ensure the full sustainability of all human activities and to regulate navigation in the newly accessible sea lanes on a multilateral basis. the arctic council, during its several years of existence, has been a model of cooperation in managing common problems. in these difficult and uncertain times, we must take this spirit and this synergy to new heights, to prevent the states of the region or other international actors from engaging in geostrategic battles, forgetting what should be the common objective: the preservation of a great shared heritage.

the regulations for the structural and cohesion funds, with two clear priorities: accelerating spending to provide more liquidity, and simplifying the rules to allow for faster implementation of
