madam president, the commitment to sustainable production has the advantage that it benefits both the competitiveness of companies and the interests of consumers in terms of quality of life and individual commitment to the environment. the eco-label is a good instrument in this respect and the reinforcing measures we are discussing here today are therefore to be welcomed. the eco-label covers a very limited number of products, is still little known by consumers and is often copied without any real accreditation behind it. i am therefore confident that the review we are undertaking in the european institutions will help to tackle these problems. we must also bear in mind another fundamental fact: the eco-label must not reflect the general norm within sustainable production; the eco-label must reflect excellence within sustainable production, which must be increasingly the majority. the challenge we face is to make our economy a green economy; the eco-label must therefore be the ultimate expression of this generalization of good practice in respect of the environment. in the committee on the internal market we had a first exchange of views this week on the report on textile product names and related labelling, for which i am the rapporteur. the textile sector is a good example of how we must not only make the approval procedures for new products, in this case new fibres, more flexible, but also strive to consolidate the eco-label, together with wider measures, so that the whole sector can move towards sustainability. only then will we be able to compete with other markets for more indiscriminate products and only then will we be able to meet the demands of consumers, which are fortunately increasingly demanding.
rapporteur. − madam president, i would like to start by sincerely thanking the rapporteurs, the shadow rapporteurs, commissioner piebalgs and ambassador reinišová for the excellent cooperation during the first three months of this year. that cooperation has been the main engine of the successful outcome we will be voting on this week. negotiations have been long, complex and sometimes tough, but i think we have managed to get an agreement that is satisfactory to all parties. regarding the overall package, as it has been negotiated, parliament can be proud of the final text. indeed, our very strong first-reading agreement on ownership unbundling gave the negotiating team a lot of leverage during the talks. this has allowed us to obtain a much tighter regulatory framework, in particular in countries with the ito model in place, where the competencies of national regulators will be increased, with independence from both governments and industry. this new role will reduce the risk of uncompetitive behaviour, especially in circumstances where vertically integrated companies abuse their position to stop investments in new capacity. furthermore, agreement has been reached on the review clause that will allow us to check, in a few years, whether all models satisfy our goals of achieving a fully competitive and legalised market. moreover, we have substantially increased the provisions on consumer protection with regard to, among other things, billing information and improved conditions for switching suppliers. finally, another big success has been the introduction of a new provision in the third-country clause, whereby the certification of a transmission system operator (tso) from a third country could now also be denied if the security of supply of the union as a whole, or that of an individual member state, other than the one where the certification is requested, is threatened. concerning the electricity regulation, i would like to make clear that this regulation plays a crucial role, since it gives member states the tools needed to significantly increase interconnection capacity within the union by the development and establishment of binding network codes to be applied by all transmission system operators to exchanges, thus removing one of the main physical barriers to the completion of the internal electricity market. the agreed text also enhances the role of the agency for the cooperation of european regulators in this process, in line with the first reading in the european parliament. i must admit that parliament hoped for a much more ambitious agency. however, we understand that this is only the first step in a long process of integration of regulatory frameworks. we have managed to include a new provision whereby the agency will be able to propose the basic criteria to be included in the granting of exemptions for new interconnections. this is particularly relevant since it is one of the main obstacles investors in new capacity face when dealing with different member states. having to follow several different regulatory procedures can sometimes lead to confusing results and put off investors – take, for example, nabucco. this regulation also establishes, and gives a defined role to, the european network of transmission system operators for electricity (entso), which will be in charge of drafting the network codes to be submitted to the agency, as well as developing coordinated mechanisms for emergency situations such as the european union-wide blackouts we have suffered in the recent past. i would like to finish by thanking all the technical staff, whose work has enabled us to obtain an agreement which, at the very beginning of the negotiations, we at times lost faith in reaching.
on behalf of the green group, mr president, when the market is not working, we have to intervene. we have once again broken a taboo: the free market is not sacred, and even less so in times of crisis, when the pocket of the european consumer suffers more than ever. with this agreement, which aims to put a limit on the abusive prices for calls and sms in 'roaming', the consumer wins, communication between european countries wins and a useful and positive europe wins. the telephone bill of millions of europeans could be reduced or, on the contrary, if the cost of an sms is only 11 cents, you could be typing all day and end up spending the same. the transfer measures are particularly positive, as they achieve a charge per second from thirty seconds onwards. the maximum prices for sms and data could have been somewhat lower, but in the interest of consensus, we have reached this transaction. i am glad that the commissioner has taken the initiative to put forward a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens.
in writing. the committee on civil liberties has asked for the management of the commission and the five community agencies falling within its remit to be approved. the committee is concerned, however, at the low level of implementation of payment appropriations in the area of freedom, security and justice compared with 2006 (60.41% in 2007 and 86.26% in 2006). we are aware, however, that the responsibility lies not so much with the commission as with the member states and that the low implementation is due, in particular, to the approval in may and june 2007 of the funds included in the framework of solidarity and the management of migration flows and to the delays in the implementation of other specific programmes (for example, the programmes on civil justice and information and prevention in the field of drugs). as i said, the committee on civil liberties has recommended that the management of:- the fundamental rights agency,- the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction in lisbon,- frontex,- eurojust, and- cepol be approved. i would like to say the following about the last two agencies:- we hope that eurojust will reduce the excessive number of carryovers and that the way in which contracts are concluded will be regulated, as the agency claims;- always taking into account the criticisms made of cepol by our committee, we do not believe that the approval of the management of this agency should be postponed. as far as we know, the director of cepol has been working closely with the committee on budgetary control and is doing what is necessary to correct the management shortcomings identified.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fishing industry is not subject to the same sanctions as the fishermen who are caught illegally. the commission has in fact been denouncing this matter lately. last week the bluefin tuna fishing season began. scientists tell us that we have long since exceeded the acceptable limits of sustainable fishing for this clearly endangered species. these days, the spanish minister for defence is in somalia, leading the operation to protect the tuna industry in the indian ocean from piracy attacks. if european tuna fishermen have to go so far from home to work, it is firstly because the closest stocks are about to collapse and secondly because we have an over-subsidised and clearly over-sized fleet that seeks profitability even at the cost of killing the main element that underpins its activity, fish. the common problem in all these cases - and in many others - is, once again, overfishing, the oversized size of the european fleet and, above all, the lack of control and of capacity to impose sanctions. that is why we are advocating in this report that the non-discriminatory and effective application of the rules should be one of the fundamental pillars of the common fisheries policy. we therefore call for an explicit ban on public aid to those who act illegally, as is the case with armadores vidal. compliance with the rules and a coherent approach are the best way to protect the interests of the fisheries sector in the long term. the policy is bound to fail if fishermen, from seafarers to traders selling fish to consumers, do not comply with the rules. fish stocks are doomed to disappear along with those who depend on them. the commission and the european parliament have on several occasions expressed regret at the low level of compliance and have called, among other things, for the member states to step up checks, to harmonise inspection criteria and penalties, and for the results of inspections to be transparent. we have also asked for the community inspection systems to be strengthened. the proposal for a regulation which forms the basis of this report addresses the necessary reform of the existing control system and makes a number of recommendations which must be added to those already in place following the adoption of the regulation on illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing or the regulation on the authorisation of fishing activities. perhaps the most important quality of a control system that applies to 27 member states is that all parties are treated equally and, above all, that all actors in the production chain - fishermen, intermediaries, buyers, people linked to the recreational fishing sector and others - feel that they are not being discriminated against, but also that they have their share of responsibility in this respect. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used in a fair and equitable manner. the proposal we are putting forward - and we also support the original commission proposal to a large extent - contains a number of aspects which would make it possible to make considerable progress in this direction. i would simply like to mention, as a point of order, the need for the community fisheries control agency to have a particularly important role to play, given its community nature and its mandate of impartiality. i therefore hope that the amendments which we have tabled at the last minute, in order to finalize the report, will be accepted by the rest of the house, as was the case in the debate we had in committee, and i hope that it will be a useful instrument to save those whom we must save, which are not only the stocks but also the populations that live off them.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all allow me to thank the rapporteur, mr romeva i rueda, who has undertaken some impressive work on this report. what is even more noteworthy is the fact that the rapporteur has undertaken to meet with numerous international and community stakeholders in several capitals. this file was complex and delicate. the commission would like to thank mr romeva i rueda for his work on this report. as you know, the current regulation on fisheries control dates back to 1993. it has since been amended a dozen times, in particular in 1998, to include the control of fishing effort, and in 2002 on the occasion of the last reform of the common fisheries policy (cfp). however, the resulting system has serious shortcomings that prevent it from being as effective as it should be. as both the european commission and the european court of auditors have highlighted, the current system is inefficient, expensive, complex, and it does not produce the desired results. this in turn undermines conservation and effort management initiatives. control failures thus contribute to the negative performance of the common fisheries policy. the main aim of the control reform is to ensure the respect of the cfp rules by building a new standard framework which will enable the member states and the commission to fully assume their responsibilities. it establishes a global and integrated approach to control, focusing on all aspects of the cfp and covering the whole chain of catch, landing, transport, processing and marketing – ‘from catch to consumer’. in order to achieve this, the reform is built on three axes. axis 1: the creation of a culture of compliance and responsibility of the sector. the aim of this objective is to influence the behaviour of all stakeholders involved in the wide range of fishing activities in order to achieve compliance through not only monitoring and control activities, but as a result of an overall culture of compliance where all parts of the industry understand and accept that playing by the rules is in their own long-term interest. axis 2: instituting a global and integrated approach to control and inspection. the proposal ensures uniformity in the implementation of the control policy, while respecting the diversity and the specific characteristics of different fleets. it establishes a level playing field for the industry by covering all aspects from capture through to the market. axis 3: the effective application of cfp rules. the reform also aims to clearly define the roles and responsibilities of member states, the commission and the community fisheries control agency. under the cfp, control and enforcement are the exclusive competence of the member states. the role of the commission is to control and verify that the member states are implementing the cfp rules correctly and effectively. the current proposal does not try to change this allocation of responsibilities. however, it is important to rationalise procedures, and to ensure that the commission has the means to actually see to it that the member states equally implement cfp rules. i would also like to emphasise the fact that the proposal will reduce administrative burdens and make the system less bureaucratic. the commission’s impact assessment found that if the reform is adopted, the total administrative costs for operators could be reduced by 51% – from eur 78 to eur 38 million – largely through the use of more modern technologies, such as the extension of the use of ers, vms and ais. existing paper-based tools will be replaced at all stages of the fisheries chain – i.e. logbook, landing declarations and sales notes – except for vessels below 10 metres overall length. for fishermen, the electronic system will make it easier to record and communicate data. once the system has been introduced, a number of reporting requirements will be removed. the system will be quicker, more accurate, less expensive and will allow for the automated processing of data. it will also facilitate cross-checking of data and information, and the identification of risks. the result will be a more rational and risk-based approach to control actions at sea and on land, the latter being inherently more cost-effective. the proposal will also remove the current obligation on member states to transmit lists of fishing licenses or fishing permits to the commission, which will instead be made accessible by electronic means to the national control services, to those of other member states, and to the commission. now turning to the report, i would like to comment on the amendments proposed. the commission welcomes the fact that the european parliament supports the legislation in principle and considers that a new control regulation is necessary. whilst the commission can go along with certain amendments that are in line with the discussion within the council working group, it considers it fundamental to retain certain key elements of the proposal. the commission can agree with an important number of amendments, in particular amendments 3, 6, 9, 10, 11, 13 to 18, 26 to 28, 30, 31, 36, 44, 45, 51 to 55, 57, 58, 62, 63, 66 to 69, 82, 84, 85, and 92 to 98. the commission cannot, however, accept the following amendments, which could be summarised as follows: concerning the monitoring of fishing activities: amendment 23 modifies the margin of tolerance to be applied to logbook catch entries to 10%, instead of 5% as in the proposal. this will seriously affect the accuracy of the logbook data that is essential when using such data for cross-checks. since such cross-checks will be used to identify data inconsistencies as indicators of illegal behaviour on which member states should concentrate their scarce control resources, this amendment would also negatively affect the operation of the computerised validation system foreseen in article 102(1) of the proposal which is considered to be the backbone of the new control system. the most important argument is, however, that fishermen can indeed estimate their catches within an accuracy level of 3%. after all, fish is stored and transported in boxes and they know how much weight of fish a box can hold. regarding amendment 29 on prior notifications, the commission believes that the idea to reserve the granting of exemptions to the council would complicate enormously the procedure and would not allow for timely reactions to developments on the ground. the commission also finds that the reallocation of unused quotas is a management matter that should be dealt with in the context of the cfp reform. thus, amendment 41 on corrective measures cannot be accepted. on transhipments of stocks subject to multiannual plans, amendment 42 deletes the entire article 33. this is not acceptable because, as you know, transhipments have been used in the past to conceal illegal catches. for that reason it is essential to maintain article 33 and that quantities to be transhipped are weighed by an independent body before they are taken on the transport vessel. amendment 47 deletes the entire section on real-time closure of fisheries. by accepting this, the commission would lose a very important instrument for the protection of stocks. real time closures are directly linked to control issues. therefore, this amendment cannot be accepted. amendment 102 is not acceptable since it deletes the article on the ability for the commission to close fisheries if so required by the commission. a similar provision exists already in the current control regulation, and it is a necessary tool to ensure that, if a member state fails to close a fishery, then the commission is entitled to close that fishery in order to ensure the respect of quotas – and this we did last year for the bluefin tuna and the year before for cod in the baltic sea. similarly, the commission cannot accept amendment 103, which deletes the provisions on corrective measures. this would weaken the role of the commission as the guardian of eu law ensuring that all member states are able to take full advantage of their fishing opportunities. moreover, this provision already exists in current legislation. as regards new technologies: concerning the vessel monitoring system (vms) and the vessel detection system (vds), amendment 19 foresees the entry into force of these electronic devices for vessels between 10 and 15 metres as of 1 july 2013, instead of 1 january 2012, as laid down in the proposal. amendment 20 foresees that the installation of vms devices and electronic logbooks is eligible for funding, with 80% cofinancing from the eu budget. regarding amendment 19, the proposal already provides for a transition period, as this obligation would only apply as of 1 january 2012, whereas the entry into force of the regulation is foreseen for 1 january 2010. since the new control system intends to make the best possible use of modern technologies, in order to develop an efficient automated and systematic system of cross-checking, it is important that these provisions apply on the date foreseen in the proposal, so as not to further delay the implementation of the new approach to control. regarding the concerns on the cost of introducing these new technologies, the cofinancing by the commission is already available under council regulation (ec) no 861/2006, which establishes cofinancing rates, and in the framework of this regulation the commission will consider increasing such rates. it would, however, go against the budgetary rules to lay down in another legislative act the rates for cofinancing. concerning recreational fisheries: on this controversial subject, i would like to indicate that, in contrast to what has been widely reported, the draft regulation does not aim to place a disproportionate burden upon individual anglers or on the leisure fishing industry. what is proposed is to subject certain recreational fisheries on certain specific stocks, namely those subject to a recovery plan, to certain basic conditions on permits and catch reporting. these requirements will also help to obtain information allowing the public authorities to evaluate the biological impact of such activities and, where necessary, to prepare the measures needed. concerning the ep report, the commission welcomes the fact that a definition of ‘recreational fisheries’ is provided for in amendment 11, and that parliament foresees that, where a recreational fishery is found to have a significant impact, catches should count against the quotas. it also welcomes the fact that the ep agrees that the marketing of catches from recreational fishing shall be prohibited except for philanthropic purposes. however, i would like to stress that it is important to maintain an obligation for member states to evaluate the impact of recreational fisheries as set out in amendment 93, and not just the possibility to do so as contemplated in amendments 48, 49 and 50. the commission, of course, wants to ensure that the final regulation adopted by the council achieves a fair balance between, on the one hand, obtaining accurate information on the impact of recreational fisheries on recovery stocks – following a case by case analysis – and, on the other, ensuring that recreational fishers, whose catches clearly have a negligible biological impact, are not burdened with disproportionate requirements. concerning sanctions and enforcement: amendment 64 inserts a new article 84(2a) indicating that as long as a holder of a fishing authorisation has been given ‘penalty points’ the holder should be excluded from receiving eu subsidies or national public aid during that time. the commission cannot accept this amendment. in the same vein, amendment 61 cannot be accepted. in fact article 45, point 7, of regulation (ec) no 1005/2008 establishing a community system to prevent, deter and eliminate illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing already provides the possibility to ban offenders temporarily or permanently from access to public assistance or subsidies. to introduce such a rule additionally in the context of the penalty point system would be disproportionate. amendment 107 deletes the minimum and maximum levels of sanctions proposed by the commission. this is not acceptable, since comparable sanctions in all member states is an important element to achieve the same degree of deterrence in all community waters and thus create a level playing field through the establishment of a common framework at the community level. the provision does not affect the discretion of member states to determine which infringements are to be characterised as serious. concerning the powers of the commission: amendment 71 imposes the presence of an official of a member state during inspections carried out by the commission, and in the same vein, amendment 108 limits the possibility for the commission to carry out inquiries and inspections only in cases where a member state has been previously informed. the capacity of the commission to undertake autonomous inspections would be seriously affected when officials of the member state concerned have to be always present during inspections. by not providing an official, the member state concerned could even prevent an autonomous inspection from taking place. amendments 104, 108, 109 and 110 are also problematic since they restrict the competencies of community inspectors, restrict their ability to perform autonomous verifications and autonomous inspections. without such competencies for community inspectors, the commission cannot ensure the same quality of application of cfp rules in all member states. amendment 72 takes away the basis according to which community financial assistance can be suspended or cancelled when there is evidence that provisions of the regulation have not been complied with. the commission cannot accept this amendment. with this amendment the simple conclusion by the commission that the member state concerned has not taken adequate measures would be sufficient to take measures against that member state. on the other hand, amendments 111 and 112 limit the competence of the commission to suspend community financial assistance. this would seriously undermine the capacity of the commission to apply this measure. furthermore, the amendment does not clarify who, instead of the commission, is supposed to take such a decision. concerning the closure of fisheries: amendment 73 limits considerably the cases in which the commission will be able to close a fishery for failure to comply with the objectives of the common fisheries policy. ‘evidence’ of non-respect will be much harder to prove than ‘reason to believe’. in order to ensure that the rules of the cfp are equally applied in all member states and to avoid a particular threat to sensitive stocks, it is important that the commission has the possibility to close a fishery when the relevant member state fails to do so itself. in the same vein, the commission cannot accept amendment 113, which proposes to delete this article. amendments 74 to 78 reduce substantially the pressure on member states to respect national quotas. acceptance of these amendments would simply mean maintaining the status quo. the amendments reduce substantially the possibility for the commission to take measures to ensure that member state fishers do not fish on a regulated stock for which the member state has no quota or has a small quota. this would be particularly detrimental in cases where such fishing effectively prevents other member states from fishing their quotas. amendments 79 and 80 delete articles 98 and 100, which give the commission the possibility of deducting quotas and to refuse quota exchange for failure to comply with the objectives of the cfp. the commission wishes to maintain this provision, which is an important instrument, to ensure the respect of the cfp rules by member states. it responds to the recommendation of the court of auditors to reinforce the capacity of the commission to put pressure on member states. it will also help demonstrate to national fishing industries that the respect of the cfp rules by their national administrations is also in their interest, and they can be expected to exert a positive pressure on their national administrations to that effect. amendment 114 proposes the deletion of article 101 on emergency measures. the commission cannot accept this amendment since this provision is an important instrument to ensure the respect of the cfp rules by the member states. i would once again like to thank mr romeva i rueda for the report and the committee for the attention it has given to this very important issue. this report is a significant contribution to a truly efficient control system. i would like to apologise for taking up so much time.
the commission's proposal is based on the principle of subsidiarity, which is the basis of the treaty of rome. it is unacceptable that the commission should continue to proclaim that its entire fisheries policy will be based on dialogue with the parties concerned and that it should be fair when drafting the regulation which has the most serious immediate consequences for the fleet when that dialogue and that prior consultation are stolen from the sector. this is a bad start in trying to establish the culture of compliance that the commission is so eager to promote. the timing is also very questionable. it is true that the control policy is one of the most glaring flaws of the common fisheries policy, but so is the fact that the commission has maintained it since 1993 and has decided to change it just when it is presenting the preliminary work for a reform of the cfp which announces a thorough review of the conservation and management system. since control is an integral part of any management system, it would have been much more reasonable to coordinate both reforms without running the risk that the 2012 reform would render this proposal obsolete, some of whose measures will not enter into force until at least that year. these two major errors undermine what could have been great successes, such as attempts to harmonize infringements and sanctions and the objective of holding member states accountable at once for the obvious lack of political will to implement control measures. i can only thank the rapporteur, mr president, for his work and i am sorry that we have so little time to work on such an important matter.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all i would like to thank you for this interesting debate. clearly we are equally strongly aware of the need for a meaningful reform of our control systems. let me try to touch on a number of points that have been raised, first of all with regard to the question concerning recreational fisheries. as i said, this is a very contentious topic, probably the most contentious of all the control provisions contained in the proposal. however, it has given rise to a number of misconceptions as to what the real objective and purpose of the provisions is. i said that we are prepared to accept the definition that is proposed in one of the amendments. i will be setting out clearly our position on the definition and on the proposed regulation of recreational fisheries in the coming days, including by writing directly to the anglers’ representatives in order to spell out the objectives, the parameters and the details concerning recreational fisheries. then, i hope, i will be receiving feedback from them and, if necessary, we will look into the provisions in order to make them more finely-tuned to the only objective that we need to target. we have a significant problem with recovery stock. there are certain recreational activities which impose big pressures on such recovery stock and we need to address this point. this is only fair for the professional fishermen that we address this. otherwise we can never hope to turn the situation around if there is pressure from a significant fishing effort, even though it is carried out in a recreational manner and no earnings are derived from it. the stock cannot hope to recover if there is significant effort, as scientific reports have indicated to us. (interjection from the floor: ‘no science for that at all!’) concerning the total lack of consultation of the sector, i think that we have consulted the industry. i myself took part in such a conference in scotland some time ago. all racs have submitted their opinions and, furthermore, as in any other legislation, we organised a public internet consultation. the sector was specifically consulted in the framework of the advisory committee for fisheries and aquaculture in the course of 2008. concerning the point made on small-scale vessels, the commission believes that the small-scale fleet can have a significant impact on resources. this is the reason why there is no general exemption for this fleet in the proposal. however, the proposal provides specific exemptions for certain categories of vessels, in general those under 10 metres, and in particular on the vms, on log book, on prior notification and landing declarations. in this regard, the proposal respects the principle of proportionality. financial aspects are also taken into account at the level of eu cofinancing of up to 95% of the costs for those electronic devices, to help the stakeholders to use the new technologies. exemptions will be examined further within the final presidency compromise. i would also like to say, with regard to the points made by mr guerreiro, that many of the points that he mentioned already exist in the existing control provisions. therefore, were we to take up the amendments that he suggests, we would actually be moving backwards with regard to control and enforcement, rather than strengthening the provisions that need to be strengthened. we are seeking a level playing field in the sanctions provisions as contained in the proposed regulation. obviously we are prepared to look into them further in order to see whether there needs to be further fine-tuning, but the main objective of the provisions on sanctions in the proposed regulation is to ensure that there are no significant discrepancies, such as exist today, between sanctions given by certain member states, or by the judicial authorities of certain member states, and sanctions that are given by the judicial authorities of other member states. finally, i would like to thank mr farage for his confidence shown in my staying here for a second term!
the rapporteur. - mr president, i would like to dedicate the last two minutes of my speech to thanking you. firstly, to the commission, not only because of the work and the opportunity: i think that it is indeed always difficult to raise a question of this nature and this dimension, but i think it was necessary, at least, to open the debate. it has done so with courage and, of course, there will always be those who think that the time is never right, but i think that at least the debate has served and will serve to make clear some of the difficulties we have in regulating this sector more and better. secondly, i would like to thank the other speakers, the shadow speakers, because, as the debate has shown, we have very different points of view and we have made a great effort to reach agreements. i want to acknowledge the effort that you have all put into this work. the endpoint we have reached may not be the one that each and every one of us would like. for example, as regards the margin of tolerance, i agree with the commission, that is to say, i think that 5% was already enough. 10% is part of this transaction, because there were other colleagues who went much further. the same applies to the possibility of extending or, in any case, extending the period for the implementation of the electronic system. i also want to remind you, because sometimes it is forgotten, that this will not be an additional cost. in any case, there are special resources for this from the commission. and as regards the last aspect, perhaps the most controversial but not necessarily the central issue of this resolution, the issue of recreational fishing, i want to emphasize one aspect, which is that of non-discrimination. if we do not understand that we all have to take our share of responsibility, it is very difficult to achieve the desired result. in the negotiation we got a transaction which was, of course, difficult, but which was, for me, quite acceptable. however, the question of whether we should voluntarily or compulsorily carry out the study on the impact that recreational fishing could have was left out of the agreement. i think that at least, given that some exceptions are being proposed for the recreational sector, it would be good if there was a possibility of a commitment - rather than an obligation, a commitment - on the part of the states to provide the necessary information, because, i insist, the responsibility is either shared or in the end everyone, including the recreational sector, will be affected by the lack of control.
the commission's proposal is a very important one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for pointing out some of the major concerns raised by the commission's proposal. one is the trend which is beginning to emerge to regulate by zone matters which are pillars of a common policy. while this approximation may in principle be understandable in the case of technical measures, it will be necessary to be very careful that subsequent regional regulations are limited to purely implementing aspects and regulating technical details. i say this because the drawing up of framework regulations containing minimum measures followed by legislation in different areas is, together with an increasing use of comitology, one of the ways in which the commission is prepared to exhaust the prospect of co-decision in fisheries matters, as dg mare itself admits without hesitation in the green paper on the reform of the common fisheries policy. and it must be borne in mind that we are not talking about any policy, but a common policy, which requires that we be very clear about what can be a more or less disguised devolution of powers to the member states or an excessive territorialization of what should be common rules designed not to distort competition and to avoid discrimination between fleets. so while it may be reasonable for very local species to have their minimum size regulated in regional regulations, those cases should be the least and the minimum sizes in general, such as mesh sizes or the criteria according to which they can be landed and sold, should be common and approved by the council and parliament. this is also the case with some of the main amendments introduced by the committee on fisheries, which seek to reduce the application of the comitology procedure to the most purely detailed aspects and insist that the council should be left with the rules for fixing the barriers, the dimensions of the nets or the measures for the elimination or reduction of discards, since we believe that all community operators should be bound by minimum rules of the game which are the same for all. it should be remembered that the only truly community policy in this so-called common policy is access to markets, whereas the conservation and management policy - let alone the control policy - leaves a margin of manoeuvre which member states often use without hesitation to benefit their fleets to the detriment of others. we have just seen the commission's strong commitment to the community and to the homogenization of controls, and it is difficult to understand how, through the rest of the measures, the same game is being dismantled, fragmented and different rules are being created for the same game depending on where it is played. this puts at risk the entire credibility of the common fisheries policy and its own future as such, something that should not be assumed before the 2012 reform. finally, as regards the controversial single-net rule, i think that parliament has offered the commission a good alternative approach indicating in which cases it may not be feasible and it should therefore be permissible to carry on board more than one fishing net. i hope that the commission can therefore be sensitive to what have proved to be major concerns of the fisheries sector and of our own committee on fisheries.
member of the commission. − mr president, let me express my thanks to the rapporteur, mr visser, ms fraga and the fisheries committee for the draft report on the commission’s proposal for technical measures for the atlantic and the north sea. this is a very technical file and, as you are aware, technical conservation measures in the atlantic and the north sea originate to a large extent from existing rules. in community legislation the measures are spread out in different regulations: the 1998 general technical measures regulation for the atlantic and the north sea; the additional technical measures regulation for the recovery of cod and hake; and the annual tac and quota regulation, which also contains a number of technical conservation measures. apart from this legal complexity, the present rules are in some cases very complicated and difficult to implement and control. the commission adopted the proposal for a new regulation on technical conservation measures for the atlantic on 4 june of last year. the proposal was drafted after extensive consultation of stakeholders and member states during 2006 and 2007. it groups together all the relevant rules into one single legislative act, which will therefore improve legal consistency. furthermore, the proposal seeks to simplify, clarify and streamline the various rules. special attention has been paid to simplifying onboard inspections and reducing the costs for fishermen. there are also some additional rules to reduce discards, such as the establishment of a legal framework for real-time closures, already applied in the north sea. a new decision-making structure is being proposed, using a council-level decision for the general and essential provisions and comitology for the more detailed and technical region-specific provisions, thereby avoiding micro-management at a political level. this new approach is not supported in your report, where amendments 1, 6, 7, 25 and 26 call for council regulations both for general and for detailed technical rules. the commission, particularly in the framework of the cfp reform, does not want to continue with micro-management measures at a political level. however, taking into account the point made in the report regarding comitology, the commission is ready to study any procedure which, while maintaining comitology for regional technical rules, will enable the raising at council level of any matter which appears to be essential or political. the commission can partially accept amendments 2 and 3, relating to additional illustrations of fishing gears, if needed, and to certain specific market provisions, particularly on the minimum size of species, with the aim of harmonising measures. in line with discard policy, the commission is proposing new rules about real-time closures and moving-on provisions for specific fisheries in order to reduce discarding practices. both measures are considered to be efficient tools and, in order to reduce discards, are important in order to allow for a switch from rules dealing with landings to provisions on real catches. for that reason, the commission cannot accept amendments 4, 5, 21, 23 and 24. however, amendment 20, only in so far as it calls for ‘quantity’ to be replaced by ‘weight’ to define the level of by-catch, is acceptable. in addition we can positively consider the second part of the amendment regarding the derogations on distance. the parameters of such a derogation, however, would have to be studied in some detail and will be laid out in the implementing regulation. the commission, mainly for inspection purposes, intends to implement the one-net-rule provision, which should be applicable to most european fisheries. the commission is ready to examine possible derogations for specific fisheries, where these are justified and well argued, and where they take into account the criteria set out in amendment 11. such derogations should be part of the regional regulations. the other aspects of the commission’s proposal are very technical, with many details related to the construction and use of fishing gears in the atlantic. i note that the rapporteur and the fisheries committee also addressed the very technical elements of the proposal and suggested a number of amendments, with the intention of improving the proposal. however, i must express my reservations regarding amendments 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 22. the technical rules proposed on the basis of scientific advice have been simplified in comparison with current legislation, and will facilitate inspection on board and reduce costs for fishermen. the commission cannot accept amendments 18 and 19, since the provisions proposed are already in force, subsequent to a political agreement in council on a proposal from the commission based on scientific advice, and no new information is available to justify any modification. i can support the idea set out in amendment 27, and therefore, when introducing new technical measures, the commission agrees to delay their entry into force so as to allow fishermen enough time to make the necessary adaptations. let me again express my gratitude to the rapporteur and the committee for their work on this proposal.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all i would like to thank mrs davis for her kind words just expressed. i would like to say that with regard to this regulation, as i said in my opening statement, the issue of comitology is aimed at simplifying the currently over-complex system of decision-making on very technical issues. however, i agree that we have to have a procedure in place that will nevertheless allow an issue to be raised at council level should any matter appear to be of a significant or political nature. on the question of discards, we have already started to take measures to reduce discards, in particular within the parameters of the north sea and of the cod recovery plan. we will continue and we will be coming up with further proposals, for example on the banning of high grading, in a general manner which we will be proposing for 2010, and we hope that we will be dealing with this issue holistically in the discussions on the reform of the common fisheries policy with a view, i hope, to the final result being the total elimination of discards. i would like myself to thank the members of parliament, in particular the members of the fisheries committee, for the constant support they have given the commission in dealing with the sometimes intricate and politically sensitive issue of fisheries.

, president of the council. mr president, madam member, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for the various contributions you have made during this debate. i want to assure you that the council is firmly committed to strengthening and completing the single market. the bureau therefore considers that it was for this very reason that the amendment of existing community legislation was necessary. the presidency also fully shares the objective of increasing the competitiveness of the road transport sector in the european union by streamlining and simplifying the existing legal framework, thereby helping to limit market distortions. but a full opening of domestic transport markets would expose our transport companies to unfair competition and would damage the functioning of the market, as there are still significant fiscal and social disparities between member states. this should be avoided, in particular in times of economic crisis, when the economy as a whole requires a careful and president of the council in office. in its conclusions of 19 and 20 march 2009, the european council noted that substantial domestic and external sources of private and public financing, in particular in the most vulnerable developing countries, will be required to finance mitigation and adaptation measures, and that the eu will contribute equitably to the financing of these measures in developing countries. commission estimates based on recent studies suggest that additional public and private investment will need to increase to around €175 billion by 2020 to reduce emissions to a level compatible with the eu target. current analyses also predict that more than half of these investments will need to be made in developing countries. the unfccc secretariat further estimates that the scale of adaptation needs in developing countries in 2030 will range from eur 23 to eur 54 billion per year. the council adopted a clear position on the financing of mitigation measures in developing countries. developing countries should develop strategies and plans for the development of a low-carbon economy with the help of developed countries. those strategies and plans should distinguish between measures that can be taken on their own, as they have zero or very low costs or even net benefits in the medium term, and measures that will lead to positive additional costs that individual countries cannot easily bear on their own. sufficient, predictable and timely financial support is essential for the implementation of the copenhagen accord. the international financial architecture providing such support shall be based on the principles of efficiency, effectiveness, equity, transparency, accountability, coherence, predictability and sound financial management. with regard to the source of funding, the european council confirmed options that could be further explored in international negotiations, a contribution-based approach based on an agreed scale, a market-based approach based on an auction arrangement or a combination of these and other options. moreover, in the transition to a global carbon market, flexibility mechanisms, the clean development mechanism and joint implementation will continue to play an important role in financing emission reductions in developing and transition economies. in this context, it will be important to strengthen environmental integrity, contribution to sustainable development and equitable geographical distribution. it is also necessary to further expand the carbon market to provide clear signals on the carbon price. this the ombudsman's office has been asked to investigate the allegations of discrimination on grounds of age in the context of the european union's fight against racism and xenophobia. the commission and parliament had taken the decision years before not to hire freelance interpreters who were older than the retirement age of their own officials. the interpreters concerned took the matter to the court, won at first instance, but on appeal the decision was reversed, albeit by default of form and without going into the substance. in the light of the background and judgments, the ombudsman rigorously examined the complaint and concluded that there was indeed discrimination and a violation of the charter of fundamental rights, and recommended that the commission change the rule in line with the behaviour already adopted by parliament following the court's ruling at first instance. the commission turned a deaf ear to the ombudsman's recommendation, which forced it to seek parliament's protection, which referred the case to the committee on petitions. there were three reasons why the committee on petitions supported the ombudsman in the resolution which was unanimously adopted in that committee: first, in line with the parliament's own conduct, which had been hiring freelance interpreters over the age of 65 whenever it seemed appropriate or necessary. secondly, the obligation to protect the ombudsman. parliament considers the ombudsman to be an institution which is sometimes uncomfortable but always indispensable in our legal system. and thirdly, we were moved to draw attention to the european commission, reminding it that it is not above other community bodies, especially those which have the responsibility of monitoring and supervising its work. we have thus come to this point, by presenting to the house the resolution which was adopted - as i say - unanimously by the committee on petitions and which calls on the commission to comply with the recommendation of the ombudsman, reiterating further that the ombudsman, together with parliament itself, is above the commission's legal service, which is an important service, but an administrative service and nothing more. nothing less, but nothing more than that. i will not hide, mr president, madam commissioner, a certain unease, because throughout this whole process we have always sought understanding, but nevertheless there have been certain pressures to prevent the report from reaching the plenary, and even now some comments suggest that parliament will not be taken into account either. this is surprising, indeed, not because of the commissioners themselves, but because of certain senior officials - a few, but some senior official - who are convinced that they are permanent staff, as opposed to members of parliament and even commissioners, who are, by definition, temporary staff and are here only on a temporary basis. i would like to say that i am very pleased that the commission has taken the initiative in this matter, and that it is not only the commission but also the council which has taken the initiative.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all, i would like to stress that the commission has acted in good faith, strictly respecting all relevant legal rules in the process. we have never been seeking a conflict with the ombudsman, and even less so with the european parliament. our opinion was that our position would be recognised by the ombudsman. our starting point is that, over the years, the working conditions for agents interprètes de conference (aics) have been increasingly aligned to the rules of the staff regulations. since 2000, freelance interpreters have been linked to the staff regulations, after the decision of the council of ministers that they can pay community tax instead of national taxes on their income from the european institutions. and then, from 2004 on, they have been covered by article 90 of the conditions of employment of other servants, which is why they are now called aics. the age limit of 65 years is a rule of the staff regulations that covers all categories of personnel working for the institutions, be they officials, temporary, contract or auxiliary staff, as well as parliamentary assistants, following the recent adoption of a new regulation in this respect. this rule was applied to aics by the commission, as well as parliament, between 2000 and 2004. following a decision of the court of first instance in 2004 stating that not to recruit aics over the age of 65 constitutes discrimination, the institutions suspended the application of the rule. however, following an appeal against the decision, the court declared it null and void. consequently the commission returned to its previous practice. as there is no longer a court decision in the matter, our reading is that the previous line applies and that the commission has to apply the rules deriving from the council regulation of the year 2000 and stop recruiting at the age of 65, exactly as for other staff. the freedom of the interpretation services of the institutions to recruit aics according to their needs is a cornerstone of efficient delivery of conference interpretation. this makes it possible to have most regular and predictable demand covered by staff interpreters, whilst fluctuating demand and peak situations are catered for by recruiting aics. this tried and tested system has made it possible for the institutions to satisfy requests for interpretation according to demand, including making a success of the latest enlargements while keeping costs under strict control. this approach also supports an active policy of training of young conference interpreters. finally, i would like to welcome the very positive contacts between parliament and the commission in this matter, and i would especially like to thank vice-president martínez martínez for his valuable contacts with my colleague commissioner orban in a previous phase.

the rapporteur. - madam president, i would like to join the other members of this house in thanking the honourable member and the commissioner for the work we have all done together, and for which i think we can congratulate ourselves today. i would also like to thank the unconditional support i have had as rapporteur for the gsm directive, in particular the shadows who have worked with me, and in particular commissioner reding for the flexibility she has shown throughout this process in giving back to parliament that role we had called for, of involvement in the strategic planning of spectrum. and of course also to the czech presidency, because it has clearly stated its willingness to resolve this directive together with the rest of the package before the end of the mandate. i believe, as rapporteur for this gsm directive, that the final solution we have given by including the strategic planning of spectrum at community level in the future multiannual programmes for radio spectrum policy, linking it to the framework directive, has been a good one. this is right because we are thereby recognising that spectrum, as a scarce public good, needs the control of the legislator and also that strategic planning in the development of new networks - wireless and optical fibre - which are - and we have all pointed this out - the future, a future in which we must offer legal certainty to operators so that they can invest and we can regain the leadership that the european union once had. it is also very important - and i would like to stress this - that we have introduced the principle of technological neutrality of the network into this general framework, because this was an exception to that principle, and we are thus giving parliament a double legitimacy in dealing with a situation of this size. i think that in this context this directive is a good example of how to give greater flexibility to spectrum management, as the reform of this telecommunications package as a whole is intended to do. we cannot forget, and i would like to point out - as some of my colleagues have done - that in the european union the turnover of services related to radio spectrum is approximately eur 300 billion, i.e. we are talking about 1.2% of community gdp. optimising the management of this scarce public resource will therefore undoubtedly be of great help, particularly in these times of economic crisis, and will undoubtedly help to overcome the crisis. i believe that this is an investment opportunity for companies to develop new services which can re-energize demand and also contribute to improving public services for citizens. in short, an efficient spectrum policy in the european union that allows us to get the most social and economic return from this resource, which we want to do at the lowest possible cost, and that offers greater business opportunity for service providers. we are all undoubtedly interested in having more and better services for consumers, which is what we are ultimately legislating for, and above all in better provision of public services for citizens, that is, in being able to work together to achieve greater social and territorial inclusion of european citizens. ladies and gentlemen, i think we can congratulate ourselves today on the completion of much needed work for a sector such as telecommunications, a sector which in 2008 continued to grow at a rate of 1.3% in real terms against a real increase of 1% in gdp in the economy as a whole. it is true that our work requires the support of all of you tomorrow, which i ask for so that we can finally have this legislative framework.

member of the commission. - madam president, thank you to everyone who has made this very important package possible. i am thinking of the rapporteurs and their collaborators, of course, but i am also thinking of the czech presidency, and i would like to say officially here that ambassador jana reinišová has been fantastic in her collaboration with parliament and the commission to make this project possible. we now have a balanced text, which allows for open markets, investment, internet freedom and the right to internet. we have a text which has potential for the development of industry and therefore for the preservation and development of employment and for users. the text balances the lisbon strategy for growth and jobs with the many advances in consumer rights for internet users. allow me to answer some of the questions which have been raised. one of the issues concerned investment in next-generation access networks by ensuring that telecom operators receive a fair return on investment, taking due account of the risk involved. it is already possible for several companies to share the investment risk under the current rules. the new rules confirm this and say at the same time that effective competition and non-discrimination rules have to be maintained. this is very important. i want to underline it because i sometimes hear only part of the story, but it is the whole story on investment which has to be applied in practice. the second question concerns data breaches. operators must assume the responsibility that comes with processing and storing these huge amounts of information. the new rules therefore introduce mandatory notifications for personal data breaches for the first time in european law. this means that communication providers will be obliged to inform the authorities and their customers about security breaches affecting their personal data. in addition, the rules concerning privacy and data protection are strengthened in such areas as the use of cookies and similar devices. internet users will be better informed about what happens to their personal data and will find it easier to exercise control over their personal information in practice. a second element concerns a more open and neutral internet for consumers. european consumers will have an ever greater choice of competing broadband service providers available to them. internet service providers have powerful tools at their disposal that allow them to differentiate between the various types of data transmission on the internet, such as voice or peer-to-peer communication. even though traffic management can allow premium high-quality services to develop and can help ensure secure communications, the same techniques may also be used to degrade the quality of communications or other services to unacceptably low levels. that is why, under the new eu rules, national telecom authorities will have the power to set a minimum quality level for network transmission services so as to promote net neutrality and net freedoms for european citizens. in the new text, we have added new transparency requirements which are of the utmost importance. the fourth element i would like to stress is the recognition of the right to internet access. the new rules explicitly recognise that internet access is a fundamental right such as the freedom of expression and the freedom to access information. the rules therefore provide that any measures taken regarding access to, or use of, services and applications must respect the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons, including the right to privacy, freedom of expression and access to information and education as well as due process. madam president, i thought it was very important to emphasize these fundamental rights because they are the basis of our european values, european values which are also based on the new telecommunications rules. and by the way, i would like to speak up because there are many parliamentarians who have spoken up about this on the freedom of the internet. the compromise is a victory for the freedom of citizens and internet users. this compromise, firstly, very clearly affirms the freedoms of our citizens as enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights, including the right of access to the internet, which is an integral part of freedom of expression and information. secondly, the compromise makes clear that the disproportionate solutions that have been proposed to restrict the rights of internet users are not legal. and thirdly, the compromise confirms that there must always be the possibility of bringing a case to a judge, an independent and impartial tribunal, whose decision must be respected. all this is in the compromise and i believe that on the basis of this compromise the work that the commission and parliament will be doing in the very near future will have a solid basis which will underline the rights of our citizens and the intrinsic values of our europe. that said, i would ask the council to act quickly so that the final version of the text, which i hope will be voted on tomorrow, can be presented as soon as possible and without delay.

member of the commission. − let me first recall that member states are, under community law, largely free to design their direct tax systems in a way that best meets their domestic policy objectives area, which means transparency, exchange of information and fair tax competition. firstly the communication identifies how good governance in the tax area could be improved within the european union so as to reinforce the argument for other jurisdictions to follow. it calls on member states to swiftly adopt commission proposals for directives on administrative cooperation and mutual assistance in the recovery of taxes and savings taxation. member states should also continue to give appropriate priority to eliminating harmful business tax regimes. more specifically, the commission’s proposal on administrative cooperation contains a provision according to which bank secrecy could no longer be invoked to deny a request for information from another member state relating to persons non-resident in the requested member state. this is entirely in line with international consensus on tax information exchange. secondly, in order to enhance the promotion of good governance beyond the european union, the communication suggests how to ensure better coherence between eu policies with a view to ensuring that the deepening of economic relations between the european union and its partner mr president, the adoption of this directive, as a first response to the financial crisis of august 2007, should not be delayed. the commission's proposal is to be implemented with caution, to avoid any sudden upheavals, and to be accompanied by a more ambitious review in the light of international developments. financial institutions need a strong capital base and to compete on a level playing field through a harmonised definition of own funds, in particular for hybrid instruments, and a proportionate strengthening of the treatment of large risks. the introduction of more transparency and alignment of the interests of the originator with those of investors in securitisation processes is essential. the retention on the balance sheet of at least 5% of securitised products, the avoidance of multiple application and the reinforcement of investor due diligence go in this direction. the creation of colleges of supervisors for cross-border groups and the strengthening of the role of the committee of european banking supervisors is a step towards more integrated european supervision.

the rapporteur, mrs schleicher, has just said that the report is a report on the situation of human rights in the world and the role of the european union in this field. firstly, the report has two distinct areas: one is a description and assessment of the unfortunately negative human rights situation in many countries and regions of the world, often bordering on or entering the territory of human tragedy; and an assessment based on the acquis, the acquis, of this parliament in taking a position on the various problems and also based on a willingness of the rapporteur to place himself in the mainstream of what the positions and actions of the various institutions of the european union are, not seeking to emphasize the elements of differentiation, but mainly the aspects of coincidence, because the rapporteur believes that it is with the convergence of positions that we gain strength and effectiveness in this slow and difficult world and work to improve the human rights situation. and then there is a second aspect on which i have placed particular emphasis, which is to try to identify certain priorities, that is to say, to build a summary of what can be the basic guiding elements of the european union's action on human rights in the world as a whole. i would point out nine points in this area which are clearly disaggregated from the body of colleagues' contributions and the overall structure of the report. the first of these places a temporary priority, or if you like, using a term which is a little grand in historical terms, the fight for the definitive abolition of the death penalty in the world. just as previous generations achieved the goal of universal abolition of slavery in the past, our perception is that today, for our contemporary generations, it is perfectly feasible to achieve the historic goal of universal abolition of the death penalty in the world and that the european union's role must be key, leading, in this field. secondly, particular emphasis is placed on what the report calls the 'feminization of the fight for human rights', i.e. it is pointed out that women are the part of humanity that is the most affected by human rights violations and that the union must pay particular attention and priority to this fact. the question of the human rights of children is also included in this priority, and the report contains a number of points which i think are quite interesting. thirdly, it calls for synergy between the community institutions. it is not good that there is a specialisation of roles - more realpolitik in the council or, possibly, in the commission, more principles in parliament - but that the positions must converge to be effective. fourthly, there is talk of the need to broaden and deepen the very positive trend of developing human rights dialogues with third countries. finally, there is talk of the need to seek alliances within international institutions to avoid situations such as that of the united nations human rights council, where the european union is sometimes a minority presence.

the rapporteur. - madam president, i have the honour to open this joint debate on five reports which are very important for establishing a common european policy on asylum. my own concerns the modification of the european refugee fund, the erf, in order to reallocate funds for the creation of a european asylum support office which will take the institutional form of a regulatory agency. the agency shall, inter alia, be responsible for facilitating and strengthening practical cooperation between member states in order to contribute to the implementation of the common european asylum system. since some of the tasks currently allocated and financed under the erf will be carried out by the office, such as the promotion of good practice, interpretation and translation services and support for the production and use of common statistics, it is necessary, in the interests of transparency and sound management of resources, to transfer part of the erf funds to the office. the current rules provide for 10% of the fund's allocation to be devoted to these tasks. the commission proposes that this percentage be reduced to 4% and that the remaining resources be transferred to the new office. the fund's financial allocation for the period 2008-2013 would thus rise from eur 628 million to eur 614 million. we agree with the commission that these figures are sufficient for the first tranche of the fund until 2013, when a further review of the fund is planned. the committee on civil liberties has been kind enough to entrust me with the pleasant task of advocating the opportunity for the creation of this office, a proposal which has been unanimously approved by the two committees concerned, the committee on civil liberties and the committee on budgets. while parliament, as we know, is reluctant to create new agencies, as a budgetary authority its main concern is the proper and rational management of the resources allocated, in this case to ensure practical cooperation between member states on asylum. it is well known that the acceptance rates of asylum applications vary considerably from one member state to another, with the resulting accumulation of difficulties for the host member state in managing them, especially for the states situated on the southern borders of the european union, which are regularly overwhelmed by the considerable number of people who suddenly arrive at their borders, bearing in mind, moreover, that among all of them it is necessary to identify those in need of protection. the offer of support for the resettlement and internal and voluntary relocation of asylum seekers is the best proof and expression of the solidarity which member states should show. that is, and must be, the main purpose of the creation of this office. madam president, i shall end here with my remarks on what concerns us now and, like you, i would like to take a few minutes, the last few minutes, to say a few words of the rapporteur. - madam president, the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs - and you yourself, madam president, with particular enthusiasm - have visited immigrant centres in different parts of europe, and have noted very different conditions and intolerable situations which need to be corrected. asylum seekers, however, are not comparable to irregular immigrants. asylum seekers are fleeing persecution; they are not attracted by economic factors, but are driven out by freedom-hating regimes. we spaniards know this well, since so many republican exiles were also welcomed in mexico, france and other countries. when the return directive was discussed, it was quite clear that this regulation would not apply to future legislation on the reception of asylum seekers; colleagues from the epp-ed also said that. i think it is essential that asylum seekers are informed in a language they understand. the limitation of information to asylum seekers in a language they understand or can be presumed to understand is a detriment to the present conditions and would not, i believe, be acceptable from a legal and human rights interpretation point of view. the right to be properly informed is fundamental, as it is the basis of all other rights. i have studied the financial burden of my proposal on material aid. my proposal calls for aid to asylum seekers to ensure a standard of living adequate to ensure their subsistence and the protection of their physical and mental health. to ask for less seems to me to be an affront to the dignity of asylum seekers. my proposal sets out the second reason for detention (article 8 (2) (b)) in the context of a prior interview in accordance with the guidelines established for detention by the united nations high commissioner for refugees. i also propose in article 9 (5) paragraph 1 that the judicial authorities review detention ex officio and, when circumstances change or new information emerges, at the request of the asylum seeker or, as i said before, in his absence, ex officio. oral amendment no 2 and transaction amendment no 5, adopted in committee, raise the problem of providing legal aid only in so far as it is necessary and free of charge, at the request of the asylum seeker. i ask for a separate vote on these two points, to return to legal aid which is closer to free, which i believe is fair. finally, if the initial proposals for social benefits for immigrants are reduced, as other groups have done in the committee vote, i think it is necessary, even in times of crisis, to guarantee effective access to the labour market. this will give them more autonomy, integrate them into the host society and reduce the social costs of living there. i would also like to thank mr
