madam president, i would like to congratulate the members of the envi committee and its chairman, mr leinen, on the work they have done so that we can have a resolution like the one we have, and which we must adopt decisively. we cannot simply say that we have had enough of sectoral agreements, because to talk of a retail agreement is to admit that we have already failed in some way. we must adopt this resolution, which has three noble aspirations. one, more obvious, is to avoid climate change, with concrete proposals for reducing emissions and with a commitment to finance, and which aims at a binding agreement, i mean, not a retail agreement. and two latent aspirations: first, to start working sooner rather than later to have a common energy policy, as we once had a common agricultural policy, because it was necessary, and, of course, the aspiration, also included, to regain the citizens' confidence in politics and politicians, which we in europe do not have any shortage of. in this sense, the success of the summit will be the success of all three aspirations. i therefore encourage the president-in-office of the council to continue his optimism and to press and negotiate as much as he can to bring others to this success. i do not know whether the rulers of this multipolar world want to be held accountable in history for not being able to reach a binding agreement, but i, as a member of parliament, and i believe all the representatives of the peoples, cannot be held accountable in history for not having been able to reach in copenhagen the binding commitment we have with humanity to prevent climate change.
in writing. - i voted against the framework directive on electronic communications networks and services because i believe it is an attack on freedom of expression and the civil rights of citizens. with the adoption of this directive, the european union allows the cutting of internet supply without the need for a prior court order. as a civil rights defender i can only oppose this decision which gives private companies the power to introduce restrictions on the use of the net and which is yet another example of the liberalisation of the european telecommunications market. furthermore, the fact that non-judicial bodies (whose nature and composition have not been specified) can dictate the cutting off of internet supply in the face of alleged illegal practices (also undetermined) undermines the presumption of innocence of citizens and opens the door to operators who restrict the rights of users, establish content filters and grant more speed to some pages to the detriment of others, de facto ending net neutrality.
in writing. - i voted in favour of a report which brings to a close all the work done on the so-called telecommunications package, two directives and a regulation which represent a fundamental step forward in the development of the information society and the protection of users' rights. the new legislation also provides clear rules and legal certainty to encourage new investments, which in turn will enable new services to be offered and new economic activities to be developed. this is therefore legislation with a major economic impact. the text finally adopted also ensures greater respect for the fundamental rights and freedoms of consumers in accessing the network by giving legal certainty to amendment no 138. the compromise adopted refers to the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, while amendment no 138 opted for the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. the latter option has a clear disadvantage: the united kingdom, poland and now the czech republic have introduced a protocol of derogation which prevents the ecj and their respective national courts from acting in the event of non-compliance, while all member states are signatories to the convention and there is no interference with national legal systems.
in writing. − on 9 november 2009, the report on the request for defence of the immunity and privileges of tobias pflüger (a7-0054/2009) was voted and adopted in the committee on legal affairs (juri) in the european parliament. this report is based on incorrect facts. the central point is: the report cites a judgment at first instance which was repealed in the meanwhile. the judgment is invalid because the munich regional court dismissed the action against tobias pflüger on 21 july 2009 in second and final instance. a conviction was not made. for this reason all reproaches are invalid. it is politically unacceptable that this report, which contains incorrect facts, was voted in the plenary today (24 november 2009). we have tried to get this incomplete and therefore incorrect report taken off the agenda, unfortunately without success. this kind of proceeding by the european parliament creates the impression of supporting the persecution of political active persons, in this case the munich ii public prosecution service against the former member of european parliament, tobias pflüger.

member of the commission. madam president, i apologize that, as this is a very interesting and multifaceted subject, i shall be a little lengthy in my introduction for the benefit of honourable members of this house. the commission has in place a robust set of eu animal and public health requirements for meat coming from third countries. for a number of years, the eu has maintained a very effective import policy which takes into account scientific developments and the current disease situation in third countries. in particular, it pays close attention to foot-and-mouth disease in exporting third countries because, as you know, the eu is free of this disease, which has the potential to cause serious economic damage. very detailed standards and requirements have been established at the level of the world organisation for animal health to prevent the spread of fmd. the wto agreement on sanitary and phytosanitary measures recognises that, while countries may use different standards and different methods of inspecting products, this does not necessarily increase the animal and public health risks. the eu cannot impose an exact replica of our internal legislative measures on third countries, just as third countries, to which we export, cannot impose their own national rules on us. we can only require that their measures have an equivalent effect to ours. let me take traceability as an example. in the eu we have very stringent rules on the individual identification and traceability of cattle. in the event of a disease outbreak, our rules facilitate the tracing of potentially infected animals to limit the spread of the disease. in addition, our rules allow us to trace and follow food or feed through all stages of production and distribution from farm to table. on the other hand, traceability rules applying to third countries exporting to the eu are aimed solely at ensuring that imported meat does not pose unacceptable risks for the eu. the scope of these rules is therefore much more limited than the rules in force in the eu. i would also like to stress the fact that the measures on traceability of cattle in the eu were adopted largely in response to the bse crisis which, as you recall, caused a dramatic drop in consumer confidence and major disruption of the internal market in relation to trade in beef. let me now take this opportunity to explain in more detail the extremely effective cascade of risk mitigation measures that we have in place for beef imports and which ensure the highest possible level of protection for eu public and animal health, while taking into account oie standards and remaining fully in line with the principles of the sps agreement. these measures can be grouped into five main levels of protection. they are so comprehensive that only 12 third countries outside europe are able to meet all these requirements, and consequently we only import beef from these few countries. firstly, imports of beef are only allowed from third countries or from certain parts of these countries which have been specifically authorised following a commission inspection to verify the competence of their veterinary authorities and the animal health situation in general. secondly, the territory of origin of bovine animals must be recognised as free of fmd by the oie and the european union. third, beef exporting countries must have an approved monitoring plan for specific residues from veterinary medical products, growth promoters and performance enhancers which are restricted or banned in food-producing animals in the eu. fourth, all imports of fresh meat must come from an approved slaughterhouse that has been authorised and listed for that specific purpose. fifth, we have specific conditions concerning meat production and storage. we have an additional layer of protection by only allowing bone in meat to come from australia, canada, chile, new zealand and the united states. for the seven other authorised countries, only deboned and matured beef without offal can be exported to the european union. this treatment ensures the inactivation of the fmd virus, should it still be present despite all the previous measures i have described, thus providing an additional safeguard. consignments of meat destined for the eu market must be certified by an official veterinarian who guarantees that all of the above conditions are fully met. when the meat consignment arrives in the eu, checks are carried out by the official veterinary services of the member states at our border inspection points. all imported meat must undergo mandatory veterinary checks at eu borders. the border inspection posts are obliged to carry out documentary, identity and physical checks. imported meat is subject to 100% documentary and identity checks at border inspection posts. in addition, a physical veterinary check is carried out on a minimum of 20% of all consignments of imported meat. furthermore, we have an additional level of protection through our ban on feeding swill or catering waste to animals throughout the eu. this measure ensures that susceptible species in the eu are not exposed to the fmd virus should it enter the eu despite all the previous measures i have described. all the measures i have described are fully harmonised. in 2006, the european food safety authority recognised that these measures are very effective at reducing the risk of fmd entering the eu. in its opinion, efsa stated, the eu thus has a sophisticated import control system in place. these efforts appear to be very effective with regard to legal trade in meat and meat products. this brings me to my next point. since the harmonization of veterinary import conditions in the 1970s, we have never had an outbreak of fmd in the eu through the legal import of meat. i am sure i do not need to remind you that the outbreak of fmd in the uk in 2001 was caused by the illegal introduction of meat most probably from asia and the illegal use of swill feeding. i therefore believe that we should focus our efforts on where the real risks are, and target illegal introductions or personal imports rather than trying to excessively regulate legal imports. in this respect i hope you have all seen the posters in eu airports and at other points of entry into the eu explaining to travellers the rules concerning the introduction of products of animal origin. i am aware that some of you have expressed concern as regards our imports of beef from brazil. i would like to remind you that additional requirements were established for imports of brazilian beef in january last year. these include, in addition to all the requirements i have already outlined, that the farms of origin are audited and approved by the brazilian authorities. the brazilian authorities now also require that bovine animals whose meat is destined for the eu market are individually identified and registered in a database. these animals represent less than 1.5% of the total brazilian bovine population, amounting to about 2.9 million animals in approved holdings. as a consequence, the brazilian authorities reassessed holdings wishing to produce beef meat for export to the eu. from a total number of more than 10 000 holdings eligible for export in november 2007, only 1 708 farms are currently approved. as a consequence, eu imports of brazilian beef have dropped dramatically. in early 2009, some deficiencies were identified during a commission inspection, and the brazilian authorities demonstrated full cooperation to address these deficiencies. in any case, the overall findings did not justify any further restriction on imports of beef from brazil. as things stand, imposing further restrictions on imports of beef from brazil could be interpreted as protectionism by some, and could lead to a challenge to our measures at the wto. we also need to bear in mind that the eu will have to face, from time to time, animal health or food safety problems, and we insist that third countries react in a proportionate manner to these problems. we should lead by example, therefore playing by the rules governing international trade. i would like to conclude by assuring the house that the commission will continue to target illegal introductions which present the greatest risk to our high standards. the commission will also maintain its current proportional approach towards imports of beef from third countries, including brazil. these will ensure we maintain our high level of public and animal health in the eu and that the eu retains its respectability at international level.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, the european union imposes the highest standards in the world on community producers in terms of food safety, health, animal welfare and the environment. european farmers are obliged to comply with these standards as a precondition for receiving union support. for the vast majority, this support does not compensate for these high costs, and there is a rapid rate of abandonment of farms. this process will be unstoppable if adequate measures are not taken. but, let's get to the point. the growing deficit in european production is being covered, of course, by imports from third countries, with brazil in the lead. given the pressure on community farmers, it would be completely dishonest to allow meat consignments to enter the community market which do not comply with the minimum requirements agreed by the european union with third countries. i would also like to point out that these requirements are lower than those imposed on our own farmers, because it would seem to be contrary to the world trade organisation to impose exactly the same standards on imports from third countries. but since this world trade organisation prevents us from extending to imports the same standards as european farmers, the commission should at least ensure that all meat crossing community borders comes from farms which have been properly controlled. it would make no sense to impede imports from countries like brazil, because there is already a community demand that must be met; mr president, on specific restrictive measures, the freezing of funds of persons and entities linked to al qaeda and against members of the governments of zimbabwe and somalia, the commission and the council stated on 5 november that, once the treaty of lisbon enters into force, these proposals would be based on article 215 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union and not article 75. article 215 provides that the council shall inform parliament of decisions providing for the interruption or reduction of economic relations, etc., but article 75 makes it clear that, where necessary to achieve the objectives set out in article 67, parliament and the council shall define, that is to say, co-decide, regulatory measures to freeze funds, assets or profits held, owned or held by natural or legal persons, groups or entities, in connection with terrorist activities. article 67 also sets out the objectives of the foundations of the area of freedom, security and justice. it therefore seems clear that, with regard to persons or entities linked to terrorist activities, the legal basis for the council's proposals for regulations should be article 75. as regards zimbabwe and somalia, the council and the commission could also consider the stuttgart solemn declaration, which provides for the optional consultation of parliament on international affairs, even where the treaties do not provide for this. it is, in short, a question of making my position clear, mr president: to claim the role of parliament's co-legislator, here and now, and to ask the council and the commission for a more reasonable explanation. that's all for now.

comes to monitoring the performance of the financial system it is very difficult to have supervisory authorities and a financial policy that serves the interests of each country, if practically all banks are not from that country and take strategic decisions in accordance with the interests of their country of origin. that said, foreign banks in those countries are behaving extraordinarily well and i have referred to this before. the absorption capacity of the structural funds must be increased. we have offered, in the current financial perspective, which you approved, a very large amount of resources, which can be channelled through the structural funds during this period of financial perspective; in many cases we are not being able to use these resources and there is still room for manoeuvre which can reach in some countries up to four points of their gdp each year: 4% of gdp per year and this money is not being used sufficiently. we need to support much more - and we need to continue to debate how to do it - the integration of infrastructure, and there are bottlenecks, in part of that region, that have not yet been overcome with infrastructure that integrates its economic space and its productive fabric sufficiently with western europe. and finally, the consequences of the crisis are being paid for more in social terms in countries which do not have a sufficient social protection system, which do not have a sufficient welfare state. this is partly because they do not have a sufficient level of growth or income or wealth, but it is also partly because - and it must be said - during the years before the crisis, in some of these countries a tax policy has been implemented, a tax policy, the less the better, and when money is needed to finance public actions there is none, because there is no income. and that is a reflection also for the future.

i am sure that i share the feeling of many of the citizens who follow us, as a lawyer and as a member of the european parliament, that this is a debate without a clear focus. so let's try to clarify a few things. firstly, we are talking about a judgment of the european court of human rights, which is not an institution of the european union, but a judicial body 'in a circle concentric with the european union, but distinct' from commitment to the rule of law, representative democracy and human rights. secondly, we are talking about a judicial decision, and no decision of this parliament can revoke or amend any decision made by a court of law. thirdly, the judgment of the european court of human rights is profoundly respectful of religious freedom and its corollary of religious pluralism. freedom of religion is part of the common constitutional traditions, of the constitutional law of the member states, and it is also a fundamental right protected by the european convention for the protection of human rights. the judgment thus argues, with sound legal foundation, for the protection of religious freedom. he doesn't deny it at all. and it is unanimously done by a prestigious court which has shaped the culture of human rights for almost 60 years. but, lastly, and this is the important point, it must be remembered that no judgment of the european court of human rights has the consequence of changing the law of any member state which has signed the european convention for the protection of human rights, because the judgment recognises a right against a violation in a particular case. and only then will it be up to the member states to take the appropriate decisions on legislative changes or policies which may be inspired by the doctrine of the european court of human rights, but in no case are they bound or compelled by any judgment of the european court of human rights. there is therefore no reason for concern in any member state. no one is obliged to change either their legislation or their public policies as a result of a specific judgment of the european court of human rights. neither italy nor any other country is therefore required to adopt any general rule as a result of that judgment. but, finally, subsidiarity has been invoked. and we have to say that subsidiarity is a rule of european law which has no application in this case, because it is completely foreign in its conception and in its application to this case. i think that a rule of european law can even be invoked which allows a vote to be postponed in the event of doubt as to the relevance of a vote which does not concern matters which concern this european parliament, as i believe is the case. it seems to me, therefore, that this debate, although legitimate, is certainly a disoriented debate which needs no alarm or, much less, protest or reversal of the judgment handed down by a court of justice which is not an institution of the european union.

in writing. - this budget does not help to solve the economic, social and environmental problems facing the eu, which have been aggravated by the crisis. the increase in social and regional inequalities, unemployment and poverty are also not taken into account. the eu budget should be used to give effective priority to convergence policies based on social progress, preserving and promoting the potential of each member state, sustainability in the use of natural resources and environmental protection, with a view to achieving genuine economic and social cohesion. my whole group rejects the idea of using the community budget for a more militaristic and neoliberal eu. that is why we denounce the increase in military expenditure included in this budget. we point out, in this connection, the need for democratic control of expenditure on the common foreign and security policy, which is a grey area outside the control of budgetary expenditure.
in writing. - there can only be a political solution to the armed conflict in the area. for this reason, the interventions of both neighbouring and other countries must cease. the conflict in the democratic republic of congo (drc) requires a diplomatic solution negotiated between the parties, in full respect of the charter of the united nations and the universal declaration of human rights. the un security council should review monuc's mandate, removing its mandate under chapter viii to avoid strengthening the congolese armed forces, which endangers the un peacekeeping mission. we call for the closure of eupol and eusec missions in the drc, which have contributed negatively to the escalation of violence and the situation in the country by training security forces which have perpetrated crimes against their own civilian population. the un resolutions on the arms embargo against the drc must be implemented, because we denounce the violation of this embargo by several eu member states. since the joint resolution tabled by the other political groups does not include these fundamental points, i have voted against it.
mr president, two items were removed from the agenda this morning. but i ask you, in connection with the resolution which we agreed in the groups, can you please clarify on the basis of which rule of the rules of procedure the question was raised and the vote was taken immediately to withdraw an item from the agenda which we were to discuss this afternoon? i think it is an important question and one which the members of parliament who are here today urgently need to know.
mr president, under rule 177 of the rules of procedure, a group or at least 40 members may request the adjournment of a debate, which is what has happened this morning in an unusual way. the rules of procedure state that if the president of the chamber intends to request an adjournment, he must be informed 24 hours in advance and the president must inform parliament immediately. i would like to ask whether this procedure has been carried out, because we are faced with an extraordinary fact: for the first time the european parliament is prevented from debating a resolution agreed by all the parliamentary groups in the face of a situation of extreme gravity such as that of mrs haidar. i therefore want to know whether this procedure was carried out and, if not, whether the resolution will be discussed next, whether the resolution we agreed on between all the groups in this parliament will be taken up and put to the vote.
mr president, i also appeal to the rules of procedure and rule 177, but we do not understand how an item can be withdrawn from the agenda if it has not been tabled before the time of debate or vote. we therefore also believe that the rules of procedure have been misapplied and we therefore call on the presidency to resolve the matter.
mr president, i want to emphasize very briefly what my colleague, willy meyer, has said about the surprise that has been caused to all of us, or to a large part of this house, by the proposal this morning, which has been voted on in a surprising way and in a way that seems to indicate that it is not in accordance with and does not respect the rules of procedure.
mr president, it is indeed a matter of order. this morning the president of the socialist group asked for a joint motion for a resolution to be withdrawn from the agenda. it is an unprecedented decision, invoking a serious reason, which is that mrs haidar's life was in danger. in view of this, my group did not want to compromise this situation, taking account of what mr schulz said. but i understand that a statement by this parliament should not endanger mrs haidar and, above all, i do not understand why it has to be made against the rules of procedure. article 177 clearly states, mr president, that it must be tabled 24 hours in advance and before the debate. (the president cut the speaker off)
on behalf of the verts/ale group. – mr president, i would have liked to start this debate by talking about the case of aminatou haidar. however, due to the reasons we already know, i cannot. in any case, the question of the eligibility rights in uganda also deserves our attention, and this reminds us that once again we are forced to adopt a new text condemning homophobia. in the past, we have adopted several resolutions on that problem, including protection of minorities and anti-discrimination policies. today, we need to add the new text to those already adopted. the only attempt by a ugandan mp to table the anti-homosexuality bill deserves a political response. this proposed law includes provisions to punish those alleged to be lesbian, gay or bisexual with life imprisonment and even the death penalty. the draft also includes a provision that could lead to the imprisonment for up to three years of anyone, including heterosexual people, who fail to report within 24 hours the identities of everyone they know who is lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender, or who supports human rights for people who are. that means that any of us would also be susceptible to be taken to court for these reasons as well. we have to remind the european union and the international organisation that sexual orientation is a matter falling within the remit of the individual right to privacy guaranteed by international human rights law, according to which equality and non-discrimination should be promoted, whilst freedom of expression should be guaranteed. we ask international donors, both governmental and non-governmental, to cease their activities in certain fields should the bill pass. i strongly reject any move to introduce the use of the death penalty. if those requests are not met by the ugandan authorities, then we should call on the council and commission to reconsider their engagement with uganda, should the bill pass into law and breaches of international human rights law take place. for that reason, i wish to remind the ugandan government of its obligations under international law and under the cotonou agreement, which call for universal rights to be respected.
mr president, i am pleased that the members of the various groups are unanimous on this ugandan law which arouses our indignation - and which i believe represents the unanimity of this parliament - and my only request when i ask for the floor is to express it with my voice, in addition to expressing it later with the vote. i agree with michael cashman and the authors and spokesmen of the groups, because the fight against intolerance, against discrimination - in this case against homophobia and, moreover, against the death penalty - means that we must be very firm and ask the commission and the council to be equally firm until we get this unjust law which is taking uganda back to the era of colonialism repealed.
